analytics.description: Detection of processes performing local or domain account enumeration by invoking account directory queries or security APIs followed by structured output of account lists. The defender observes command execution or API invocation patterns that retrieve account information and produce enumeration artifacts shortly afterward.

mutable_elements.description: Match variations in enumeration commands like 'net user', 'Get-ADUser', 'dsquery'.
Short burst of account enumeration commands may indicate automation.
Restrict to non-admin accounts or unexpected users executing enumeration commands.

analytics.name: Analytic 1613
analytics.description: Enumeration of users and groups through suspicious shell commands or unauthorized access to /etc/passwd or /etc/shadow.

mutable_elements.description: Tune based on file paths such as '/etc/passwd', '/etc/group', '/etc/shadow'.
Filter known admin processes to reduce false positives.

analytics.name: Analytic 1614
analytics.description: Detection of account enumeration through directory service queries or system utilities accessing account metadata stores, followed by structured enumeration output.

mutable_elements.description: Tune for dscl -list, dscacheutil -q user, id -un, etc.
Alert if enumeration is performed in non-console session or by unusual users.

analytics.name: Analytic 1615
analytics.description: Detection of enumeration of identity entities through cloud provider APIs where principals retrieve account metadata such as IAM users or roles in rapid succession.

mutable_elements.description: Tune based on which IAM APIs are used and their frequency.
Differentiate user-initiated from automated/scripted enumeration.

analytics.name: Analytic 1616
analytics.description: Detection of identity directory enumeration through API calls or administrative queries retrieving multiple account objects within a short interval.

mutable_elements.description: Detect user vs role enumeration. Tune based on query scope.
Correlate enumeration with unexpected app registrations or identities.

analytics.name: Analytic 1617
analytics.description: Detection of enumeration activity when system processes query ESXi host account configuration or management APIs to retrieve user account listings.

mutable_elements.description: Tune based on known enumeration commands: 'vim-cmd vimsvc/auth/userlist'.
Elevated enumeration from vpxuser or root may indicate threat activity.

analytics.name: Analytic 1618
analytics.description: Account enumeration via bulk access to user directory features or hidden APIs.

mutable_elements.description: Tune based on enumeration from directory endpoints such as /users, /groups.
Detect scripted enumeration via curl/wget or unknown tools.

analytics.name: Analytic 1619
analytics.description: Account discovery via VBA macros, COM objects, or embedded scripting.

mutable_elements.description: Alert on auto-running macros accessing directory or user info.
Focus on macros invoking LDAP, ADODB, or WMI queries.

strategies.name: Local Account Enumeration Across Host Platforms

analytics.name: Analytic 0846
analytics.description: Adversary enumeration of local user accounts using Net.exe, WMI, or PowerShell.

mutable_elements.description: Detects variations of 'net user', 'net localgroup', 'Get-LocalUser'.
Restrict monitoring to low-privileged or unexpected users executing enumeration.
Tune for bursts of enumeration commands in short succession.

analytics.name: Analytic 0847
analytics.description: Enumeration of local users or groups via file access (/etc/passwd) or commands like id, groups.

mutable_elements.description: Monitors sensitive file access such as '/etc/passwd', '/etc/group'.
Restrict detection to user-initiated sessions or specific parent processes.

analytics.name: Analytic 0848
analytics.description: Enumeration of macOS local users using dscl, id, dscacheutil, or /etc/passwd access.

mutable_elements.description: Monitor dscl . list /Users, dscacheutil -q user, id -un.
Focus on enumeration from non-console users or untrusted apps.

analytics.name: Analytic 0849
analytics.description: Enumeration of local ESXi accounts using esxcli or vSphere API from unauthorized sessions.

mutable_elements.description: Look for 'esxcli system account list' and API calls from unusual sources.
Restrict detection to interactive sessions vs. maintenance/automation jobs.

strategies.name: Domain Account Enumeration Across Platforms

analytics.name: Analytic 0363
analytics.description: Adversary enumeration of domain accounts using net.exe, PowerShell, WMI, or LDAP queries from non-domain controllers or non-admin endpoints.

mutable_elements.description: Detect variations of 'net user /domain', 'Get-ADUser', 'Get-ADGroupMember'.
Tune detection for bursts of enumeration commands or search queries.
Restrict detection to non-DC or non-admin systems where such commands are unexpected.

analytics.name: Analytic 0364
analytics.description: Domain account enumeration using ldapsearch, samba tools (e.g., 'wbinfo -u'), or winbindd lookups.

mutable_elements.description: Detect suspicious use of ldapsearch, wbinfo, getent passwd, or samba enumeration tools.
Tune for high-volume or broad-scope LDAP queries.
Apply filters for unexpected users or service accounts executing the behavior.

analytics.name: Analytic 0365
analytics.description: Domain group and user enumeration via dscl or dscacheutil, or queries to directory services from non-admin endpoints.

mutable_elements.description: Match patterns such as 'dscl /Active\ Directory/All\ Domains -list /Users'.
Flag this activity only on non-directory hosts or non-admin accounts.

strategies.name: Enumeration of Global Address Lists via Email Account Discovery

analytics.name: Analytic 0641
analytics.description: Enumeration of global address lists or email account metadata via PowerShell cmdlets (e.g., Get-GlobalAddressList) or MAPI/RPC from non-admin, non-mailserver systems.

mutable_elements.description: Match variations of Get-GlobalAddressList, Get-Recipient, and related cmdlets.
Suppress expected usage on Exchange servers or known IT admin consoles.
Detect bulk execution patterns in short intervals, often used during recon.

analytics.name: Analytic 0642
analytics.description: Suspicious querying of organization-wide directory data via Google Workspace Directory API or Outlook GAL sync in high volume from abnormal users, service accounts, or unknown device contexts.

data_components.name: User Account Authentication
data_components.channel: Unusual Token Usage or Application Consent

data_components.name: User Account Metadata
data_components.channel: Directory API Access: users.list or groups.list

data_components.name: Application Log Content
data_components.channel: GAL Lookup or Address Book download

mutable_elements.description: Set thresholds for excessive use of 'users.list' or recursive group enumerations.
Flag non-admin or previously unseen user agents requesting directory information.
Distinguish between sanctioned sync tools and unauthorized scripts or OAuth tokens.

strategies.name: Cloud Account Enumeration via API, CLI, and Scripting Interfaces

analytics.name: Analytic 1087
analytics.description: Enumeration of identity roles and users via API calls such as `Get-MsolRoleMember`, `az ad user list`, or Graph API tokens from unauthorized users or automation accounts.

mutable_elements.description: Flags excessive or abnormal use of directory read scopes by unexpected principals.
Differentiate authorized automation from rogue access tokens or external tools.
Trigger correlation across short bursts of high-volume enumeration.

analytics.name: Analytic 1088
analytics.description: Use of AWS CLI (`aws iam list-users`, `list-roles`), Azure CLI (`az ad user list`), or GCP CLI (`gcloud iam service-accounts list`) from endpoints or cloud shells where such activity is unexpected.

mutable_elements.description: Suppress known admin accounts and alert on developer/test/service identities.
Correlate unexpected CLI user-agents and geolocation anomalies.
Suppress noise from known IP ranges or whitelisted accounts per region.

analytics.name: Analytic 1089
analytics.description: Bulk enumeration of cloud user email identities through `Get-Recipient`, `Get-Mailbox`, `Get-User`, or Graph API directory listings by abnormal accounts or suspicious sessions.

mutable_elements.description: Tune threshold for recipient/mailbox queries by volume per hour.
Match known admin consoles and exclude sanctioned tools like MSOL PowerShell.
Elevate sessions from unmanaged or external endpoints.

analytics.name: Analytic 1090
analytics.description: Access to organizational directories via Google Workspace Directory API, Slack SCIM, or Okta SCIM by apps or identities outside normal roles.

mutable_elements.description: Detect rapid enumeration attempts or recursive group expansion.
Tag expected SCIM clients and suppress false positives from enterprise sync tools.
Trigger alerts if enumeration occurs from anomalous IPs or regions.

strategies.name: Detection of Proxy Infrastructure Setup and Traffic Bridging

analytics.name: Analytic 1229
analytics.description: Suspicious process spawning (e.g., `rundll32`, `svchost`, `powershell`, or `netsh`) followed by network connection creation to internal hosts or uncommon external endpoints on high or non-standard ports.

mutable_elements.description: Legitimate system processes that may rarely spawn network-capable child processes (e.g., `rundll32`, `svchost`).
Watch for high-numbered ports or well-known proxy ports like 1080, 8080, 4444.
Capture unusual spikes in outbound connections over a short period.

analytics.name: Analytic 1230
analytics.description: User-space tools (e.g., `socat`, `ncat`, `iptables`, `ssh`) used in non-standard ways to establish reverse shells, port-forwarding, or inter-host connections. Often chained with uncommon outbound destinations or SSH tunnels.

mutable_elements.description: Shell piping into tools like `socat`, `ncat`, or `openssl` for tunnel creation.
Flag connections made from internal systems to uncommon high ports externally.
Capture low-privilege or unexpected users executing system-level network tools.

analytics.name: Analytic 1231
analytics.description: AppleScript, LaunchAgents, or remote login services (`ssh`, `networksetup`) establishing proxy tunnels or dynamic port forwards to external IPs or alternate local hosts.

mutable_elements.description: Identify suspicious domains often associated with CDN-routed or anonymized endpoints (e.g., Cloudflare, Fastly).
Alert when AppleScript or Automator tools are used for network tunneling tasks.
Monitor for LaunchAgents executing proxy tools or dynamic ports.

analytics.name: Analytic 1232
analytics.description: Direct use of `nc`, `socat`, or reverse tunnel scripts initiated by abnormal user contexts or unauthorized VIBs initiating connections from hypervisor to external systems.

mutable_elements.description: Custom proxy or port forwarding scripts executed from ESXi shell.
Unusual outbound connections from ESXi host, particularly to internet.
Root or elevated users initiating unexpected tunnels.

analytics.name: Analytic 1233
analytics.description: Dynamic or static port forwarding rules added to route traffic through an internal host, or configuration changes to proxy firewall rules not aligned with baselined policy.

mutable_elements.description: Focus on new allow/permit rules with dynamic NAT or port forwarders.
Flag any non-admins initiating proxy config changes.
Detect sharp changes in bi-directional traffic patterns.

strategies.name: Internal Proxy Behavior via Lateral Host-to-Host C2 Relay

analytics.name: Analytic 0204
analytics.description: Anomalous process (e.g., `rundll32`, `svchost`, `cmd`) initiates connections to internal peer hosts not seen in typical communication baselines, used to proxy or forward traffic internally, often using SMB, RPC, or high ports.

mutable_elements.description: Tune based on known host-to-host communications that are rare (e.g., workstation-to-workstation).
Focus on unusual internal traffic on ports like 1080, 8080, 4444, or SMB over non-standard ports.
Correlate unusual traffic bursts with new process execution.

analytics.name: Analytic 0205
analytics.description: `socat`, `ssh`, `iptables`, or `ncat` invoked from user space or cron jobs to create port forwarding, reverse shells, or inter-host tunnels between compromised Linux systems. Behavior is typically paired with socket activity and high entropy traffic.

mutable_elements.description: Alert on unexpected users executing inter-host relay tools (e.g., `www-data`, `backup`).
Adjust to watch for commonly misused internal TCP/UDP ports.
Shell pipelines or wrapped invocations like `bash -c 'socat ...'`

analytics.name: Analytic 0206
analytics.description: Execution of AppleScript or Automator services launching `ssh -L`, `socat`, or `launchctl` items that dynamically reroute traffic from one Mac endpoint to another. LaunchAgents used to establish permanent internal tunnels.

mutable_elements.description: Directory where proxying LaunchDaemons may be dropped, e.g., `/Library/LaunchDaemons/`.
Dynamic port forwards often use ephemeral or non-standard service ports.
May trigger on less common scripting interfaces for traffic redirection.

analytics.name: Analytic 0207
analytics.description: ESXi shell execution of tools/scripts (`nc`, `socat`, `perl`) relaying network traffic to other internal hosts, especially when initiated by unauthorized users or VMs.

mutable_elements.description: Watch for chained shell commands building local-to-local connections.
Correlate to which VM initiated the traffic tunnel; unexpected VM behavior may be suspicious.
Unusual east-west communication patterns among VMs.

analytics.name: Analytic 0208
analytics.description: Configuration of internal NAT or proxy rules that redirect traffic between client segments internally (e.g., site-to-site port forwarding). Often used to relay internal beaconing or move traffic laterally through trust zones.

mutable_elements.description: Internal subnets or endpoint roles allowed for port forwarding.
Detect changes made outside scheduled or authorized windows.
Volume of data relayed through proxy exceeds historical norms.

strategies.name: External Proxy Behavior via Outbound Relay to Intermediate Infrastructure

analytics.name: Analytic 0922
analytics.description: Unusual process (e.g., `rundll32`, `mshta`, `wscript`, or custom payloads) initiates network connection to external IPs/domains that proxy C2 traffic, often over uncommon ports or high entropy HTTP/S connections.

mutable_elements.description: Adjust for known benign but high-risk infrastructure (e.g., hosting providers like DigitalOcean, OVH, etc.).
Detect suspicious lineage—proxy tools launched from script interpreters or LOLBins.
Tune based on expected randomness in outbound request payloads.

analytics.name: Analytic 0923
analytics.description: `curl`, `wget`, `ncat`, `socat`, or custom binaries initiate outbound traffic to Internet-based proxies (e.g., via VPS or CDN). Behavior may include reverse shell constructs or persistent outbound beacons.

mutable_elements.description: Regex or command substring matches indicative of dynamic proxy setup.
Tunable list of IPs or ASNs related to known proxy/VPS abuse.
Unexpected users running networking tools (e.g., www-data, apache).

analytics.name: Analytic 0924
analytics.description: AppleScript or terminal sessions launch tools (`curl`, `nc`, `ssh`) to external IPs not commonly accessed. Outbound connections are made by LaunchAgents/LaunchDaemons, often masquerading as system services.

mutable_elements.description: Detect persistence used to restart proxy after reboot.
Often high or non-standard ports, configurable for outbound proxy detection.
Flag unsigned or anomalous binaries making external connections.

analytics.name: Analytic 0925
analytics.description: ESXi shell or guest VM tools initiate external connections via scripted traffic forwarding to Internet-based proxies. Detected by firewall or shell audit logs showing outbound connection spikes from hypervisor or guest VM to remote proxy nodes.

mutable_elements.description: Detect when VMs communicate with Internet IPs not in workload profiles.
Regex for proxy-related tools/scripts executed on the host.
Outbound only connections from ESXi to new IPs.

analytics.name: Analytic 0926
analytics.description: Changes to NAT/firewall policies enabling outbound port forwarding from internal IPs to Internet-based proxy endpoints. Log spikes in outbound flows to CDN, VPS, or anomalous ASNs with few return packets.

mutable_elements.description: Number of flows or bytes transferred per minute—flag surges to unrecognized ASNs.
Proxy destination categories: CDN, TOR exit node, anonymous hosting.
Track if unexpected user or automation changed NAT/forwarding rules.

strategies.name: Multi-hop Proxy Behavior via Relay Node Chaining, Onion Routing, and Network Tunneling

analytics.name: Analytic 1020
analytics.description: Suspicious processes (e.g., Tor clients, relays, unknown binaries) launch with sustained encrypted outbound traffic to known anonymity infrastructure (e.g., Tor, I2P), and may relay to additional internal systems via reverse proxying, ICMP tunneling, or socket forwarding.

data_components.name: Network Traffic Flow
data_components.channel: Outbound resolution to hidden service domains (e.g., `.onion`)

mutable_elements.description: Can be tuned to `.onion`, I2P, or suspicious CDN domains.
Detect known-good vs. abnormal launching binaries (e.g., mshta spawning Tor).
Threshold for persistent connections over known relay ports (e.g., 9050).

analytics.name: Analytic 1021
analytics.description: Tools such as `tor`, `nglite`, `proxychains`, `chisel`, or custom daemons repeatedly initiate outbound sessions to multiple nodes before final destination. This behavior is abnormal for Linux services outside of VPN, monitoring, or CDN relay contexts.

mutable_elements.description: Match known proxy tools, tuned for environment.
Detect outbound chaining behavior through >2 IPs in short succession.
Allow filtering by ICMP, TCP/443, UDP for obfuscation channels.

analytics.name: Analytic 1022
analytics.description: LaunchAgents or LaunchDaemons initiate persistent Tor or relay processes that make encrypted outbound connections. May be paired with sandbox bypasses or unsigned executables communicating over SOCKS proxies.

mutable_elements.description: Regex for masking patterns in LaunchAgents with proxy behavior.
Allow for exceptions for known unsigned binaries.
Monitor local 9050/9150 activity and rerouted system traffic.

analytics.name: Analytic 1023
analytics.description: Outbound encrypted traffic initiated from hypervisor shell or via VM backdoor mechanisms to relays in VPS infrastructure, especially if traversing multiple nodes before reaching Internet destination. Packet captures or firewall logs show non-VM communication paths.

mutable_elements.description: Threshold on number of IPs contacted in sequence without DNS resolution.
Flag if relay communication initiated by ESXi shell or unknown VM agent.
Filter for known Tor/VPS egress networks.

analytics.name: Analytic 1024
analytics.description: Encrypted traffic or ICMP tunneling from border routers to internal routers or unknown external IPs. Forwarded traffic shows consistent hop-to-hop relaying without matching configured VPN or expected network topology.

mutable_elements.description: Define allowed internal router communication paths.
High entropy ICMP payloads may indicate tunneling activity.
Track known multi-hop pattern signatures or port hopping techniques.

strategies.name: Domain Fronting Behavior via Mismatched TLS SNI and HTTP Host Headers

analytics.name: Analytic 0564
analytics.description: Suspicious outbound HTTPS connections where the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI) does not match the HTTP Host header, indicating potential use of domain fronting to mask C2 traffic via CDNs.

mutable_elements.description: Define acceptable mismatch ratio between SNI and HTTP Host fields based on legitimate domain usage patterns.
Whitelist of known safe CDN front-end domains (e.g., `cdn.company.com`).
Filter for suspicious initiators of domain fronting, e.g., scripting engines, lolbins, unknown binaries.

analytics.name: Analytic 0565
analytics.description: Applications such as `curl`, `wget`, or custom binaries initiate HTTPS connections where the TLS SNI is mismatched or absent while HTTP Host targets CDN-available C2 endpoints.

mutable_elements.description: Detect TLS sessions where SNI is empty—'domainless' fronting.
Environmental tuning for known binaries using alternate SNI for testing (e.g., API tests).
Enrich command-line arguments or parent-child lineage to detect abuse.

analytics.name: Analytic 0566
analytics.description: Unsigned or user-space apps initiate TLS connections with one hostname and HTTP headers requesting a different domain, commonly abused in CDN-resident domain fronting techniques.

mutable_elements.description: Helps tune detection when unsigned apps initiate fronted sessions.
Threshold to flag inconsistent domain targeting in encrypted sessions.
Alert on unusual ports used in HTTPS+SOCKS activity patterns.

analytics.name: Analytic 0567
analytics.description: Traffic originating from ESXi hosts or management interfaces displays SNI-to-Host mismatch behavior, particularly anomalous given typical infrastructure communication patterns.

mutable_elements.description: ESXi hosts should rarely initiate external HTTPS—threshold to alert.
Define entropy or timing anomalies for TLS handshake.
SNI/Host mismatch occurrence tolerance.

strategies.name: Removable Media Execution Chain Detection via File and Process Activity

analytics.name: Analytic 0841
analytics.description: Execution of files originating from removable media after drive mount, with correlation to file write activity, autorun usage, or lateral spread via staged tools.

data_components.name: File Access
data_components.channel: Suspicious file execution on removable media path

mutable_elements.description: Detect activity on mounted drives typically used by USB (e.g., E:, F:, G:). Tune based on enterprise usage.
Set timing threshold for execution shortly after drive mount (e.g., < 5 minutes).
Restrict detection to suspicious process lineage like explorer.exe, powershell.exe, or unsigned binaries.
Use entropy thresholding to detect packed/obfuscated payloads dropped to removable media.

strategies.name: Cross-host C2 via Removable Media Relay

analytics.name: Analytic 0247
analytics.description: Behavioral sequence where removable media is mounted, files are written/updated, and subsequently read/executed on a separate host, suggesting removable-media relay communication.

mutable_elements.description: Adjust drive letters used in detection (e.g., E:, F:, G:) depending on enterprise usage.
Tunable window for file write on one host followed by file read or execution on another (e.g., within 10 minutes).
Common naming schemes for payload, tasking, or exfil files (e.g., task.txt, beacon.log, data.bin).

analytics.name: Analytic 0248
analytics.description: Detection of file write-access to USB-mount directories (e.g., /media/, /run/media/) followed by same-file access or execution on another host.

mutable_elements.description: Typical mount paths to monitor (e.g., /media/usb*, /run/media/username/*).
Tunable detection window to correlate read/write between different hosts within a short interval (e.g., <15m).

analytics.name: Analytic 0249
analytics.description: Correlates removable volume mounts (disk arbitration) with file I/O events on that volume, followed by same file execution shortly after insert.

mutable_elements.description: Known suspicious USB volume labels or types (e.g., NO NAME, SECUREDATA).
Unusual processes accessing USB drives (e.g., bash, Python, unsigned binaries).

strategies.name: Detection of Non-Application Layer Protocols for C2

analytics.name: Analytic 1254
analytics.description: Anomalous use of ICMP or UDP by non-network service processes for data exfiltration or remote control, especially if traffic bypasses proxy infrastructure or shows unusual flow patterns.

mutable_elements.description: Processes normally allowed to use ICMP/UDP (e.g., ping.exe, DNS resolver).
Suspicion if client sends much more data than it receives (e.g., >90%).
Baseline which protocols are normal per host or segment (ICMP, UDP, etc.).

analytics.name: Analytic 1255
analytics.description: ICMP or raw socket traffic generated by user-mode processes like bash, Python, or nc, typically using `ping`, `hping3`, or crafted packets via libpcap or scapy.

mutable_elements.description: Uncommon programs using raw sockets (e.g., netcat, Python, nmap).
Tunable window for correlating execution with network events (e.g., 2m).

analytics.name: Analytic 1256
analytics.description: Unsigned binaries or interpreted scripts initiating non-standard protocols (ICMP, UDP, SOCKS) outside of baseline network behavior.

mutable_elements.description: Detection threshold for unsigned or transient binaries making ICMP/UDP calls.

analytics.name: Analytic 1257
analytics.description: VMCI (Virtual Machine Communication Interface) traffic between guest and host, or between VMs, originating from non-management tools or unauthorized binaries.

mutable_elements.description: Monitor for non-vSphere or VMware-native processes using VMCI.
Baseline pattern of guest-to-host traffic vs anomaly (unexpected port, volume).

analytics.name: Analytic 1258
analytics.description: Non-standard port/protocol pairings or low-entropy ICMP traffic resembling tunneling patterns (e.g., fixed-size pings with delays).

mutable_elements.description: ICMP/UDP packet content entropy filter to identify encoded payloads.
Long ICMP/UDP sessions beyond expected limits (e.g., >5min).

strategies.name: Account Manipulation Behavior Chain Detection

analytics.name: Analytic 0265
analytics.description: Account attribute changes (e.g., password set, group membership, servicePrincipalName, logon hours) correlated with unusual process lineage or timing, indicating privilege escalation or persistence via valid accounts.

mutable_elements.description: Time between suspicious process and account change (e.g., 5m).
Customize group list (e.g., Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins) to monitor.
Flag if account modifier != modified user (potential hijack).

analytics.name: Analytic 0266
analytics.description: Use of native tools or scripting (e.g., `usermod`, `passwd`, `groupmod`) to escalate permissions or persist access on existing users, correlated with login or process events.

mutable_elements.description: Common sudo or privilege escalation paths (e.g., `/usr/bin/passwd`).
Detect if user shell is changed to unusual one (e.g., /bin/sh -> /bin/bash).

analytics.name: Analytic 0267
analytics.description: Modifications to user accounts via `dscl`, `pwpolicy`, or System Preferences CLI (`sysadminctl`) that alter user groups, enable root, or bypass MDM restrictions.

mutable_elements.description: Track known non-system user UIDs or service accounts.
List of sensitive groups (admin, _developer, _analyticsd).

analytics.name: Analytic 0268
analytics.description: Modifications to SSO/SAML user attributes (e.g., `isAdmin`, `role`, MFA bypass, App assignments) often through CLI, API, or rogue IdP apps.

data_components.name: User Account Modification
data_components.channel: User Attribute Modified / Role Assignment Changed

mutable_elements.description: Expected user-role pairings per app or org unit.
Caller identity or IP address ranges for identity admin actions.

analytics.name: Analytic 0269
analytics.description: Addition of new users or changes to role permissions (e.g., ReadOnly -> Admin) via API or vSphere Client, particularly from non-jumpbox IPs.

mutable_elements.description: Expected account name patterns for ESXi/vCenter admins.
Expected IPs/subnets for legitimate ESXi access.

analytics.name: Analytic 0270
analytics.description: Role escalation (e.g., Editor → Owner) in cloud collaboration tools (Google Workspace, O365) or file sharing apps to maintain elevated access.

data_components.name: User Account Modification
data_components.channel: Admin Activity > Role Change or Sharing Change

mutable_elements.description: Threshold for labeling sensitive document access escalation.
Track changes made across organizational boundaries (e.g., guest users).

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Additional Cloud Credentials in IaaS/IdP/SaaS

analytics.name: Analytic 1469
analytics.description: Addition of credentials (keys, app passwords, x.509 certs) to existing cloud accounts, service principals, or OAuth apps via portal or API by non-standard identities or IP ranges.

data_components.name: User Account Modification
data_components.channel: Add service principal credentials, app password added, app role assignment

mutable_elements.description: App password or legacy auth activity bypassing MFA policies.
Expected IPs allowed to perform admin identity operations.
Track types like `client_secret`, `certificate`, `password`, `federated`.

analytics.name: Analytic 1470
analytics.description: Cloud API usage to create/import SSH keys or generate new access keys (CreateAccessKey, ImportKeyPair, CreateLoginProfile) from non-console access or unusual principals.

mutable_elements.description: Track root, federated identities, and STS tokens separately.
Time between key creation and first use (default: 5 min).
Expected services/accounts allowed to create keys.

analytics.name: Analytic 1471
analytics.description: Credential-related configuration changes in productivity apps, such as API key creation in Google Workspace, app tokens in Slack, or user-level OAuth credentials in M365.

data_components.name: User Account Modification
data_components.channel: API Key Created, OAuth Client Registered

mutable_elements.description: Detect suspicious redirect URI mismatches in new clients.
Highlight credentials granting excessive read/write org-wide.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Addition of Email Delegate Permissions

analytics.name: Analytic 1051
analytics.description: Detection of anomalous or unauthorized mailbox delegation activity (e.g., Add-MailboxPermission, Default/Anonymous mailbox permissions, Gmail delegation setup).

mutable_elements.description: Threshold for unexpected delegate roles such as FullAccess or SendAs.
Mailbox folder targeted by delegation (Inbox, Root, Calendar, etc.).
Pairings of delegate and delegator users that are expected.
Spike in outbound mail after delegate addition, used to catch phishing or mass exfil.

analytics.name: Analytic 1052
analytics.description: Execution of PowerShell commands that modify mailbox permissions using Exchange cmdlets (e.g., Add-MailboxPermission), often tied to BEC or post-compromise persistence.

mutable_elements.description: Exchange cmdlets to include or exclude based on scope (e.g., Add-MailboxPermission, Set-MailboxFolderPermission).
Flag suspicious script or interactive shell launch by non-admins.
Window in which Add-MailboxPermission is followed by anomalous usage (e.g., SendAs events).

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Role Addition to Cloud Accounts

analytics.name: Analytic 0771
analytics.description: Detection of new IAM roles or policies attached to a user/service in AWS/GCP/Azure outside normal patterns or hours, often following account compromise.

mutable_elements.description: IAM Role type or privilege level assigned (e.g., Admin, Billing, Viewer)
User, service account, or external federated identity context performing the action
How quickly multiple roles or policies are added after initial access
Cross-account roles from outside trusted tenant list

analytics.name: Analytic 0772
analytics.description: Behavioral chain of a user being granted elevated privileges or roles in Entra ID or Okta following suspicious login or account creation activity.

data_components.name: User Account Modification
data_components.channel: Add member to role, Add app role assignment

mutable_elements.description: Number of accounts allowed to hold sensitive roles like Global Admin
Mechanism by which role was added (PowerShell, API, UI)
Expected user-to-role mapping defined by org policy

analytics.name: Analytic 0773
analytics.description: Detection of new admin or role assignment actions within Microsoft 365/O365 environments to elevate access for persistence or lateral movement.

mutable_elements.description: Admin role type or application role granted
Time between initial login and privilege change
Was the role assignment local or via federated SSO account

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for SSH Key Injection in Authorized Keys

analytics.name: Analytic 0350
analytics.description: Adversary attempts to gain persistence by modifying ~/.ssh/authorized_keys via shell, text editor, echo or redirected output.

mutable_elements.description: Temporal window to correlate file writes and suspicious process launches (e.g., <60s)
Expected user-to-process correlation (e.g., root writing to non-root authorized_keys)

mutable_elements.description: Specific writable directories to monitor (e.g., %TEMP%, C:\ProgramData, installer unpack paths).
Known good hashes of installer binaries to detect replacement.
Correlation interval between file overwrite and execution event.
Differentiate expected admin-installer execution vs. anomalous user writes.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Hijack Execution Flow: Dynamic Linker Hijacking

analytics.name: Analytic 1209
analytics.description: Detection focuses on identifying abuse of LD_PRELOAD and related linker variables. Defender perspective: monitor unexpected setting or modification of LD_PRELOAD in shell initialization scripts or environment exports, file creation of suspicious shared libraries, and correlation of these modifications with anomalous process execution. Key signals include execve events with LD_PRELOAD defined, newly created .so files in user directories, and processes hooking libc functions exhibiting abnormal behavior.

data_components.name: Process Creation
data_components.channel: execve with LD_PRELOAD or linker-related environment variables set

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: creation of .so files in non-standard directories (e.g., /tmp, /home/*)

mutable_elements.description: Environment variables like LD_PRELOAD, LD_LIBRARY_PATH. Defenders can tune based on development vs. production systems.
Non-standard library paths (e.g., /tmp, user home dirs). May be tuned to reduce false positives from benign development activity.
Timeframe to correlate suspicious library creation with process execution that loads it.

analytics.name: Analytic 1210
analytics.description: Detection centers on DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES and DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH abuse. Defender perspective: monitor for modification of these environment variables in shell or plist files, file creation of dylibs in user-controlled paths, and correlation of environment variable usage with unexpected module loads by user applications. Suspicious indicators include processes with DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES set, execution of applications loading untrusted dylibs, and anomalies in module load history.

data_components.name: Module Load
data_components.channel: loading of unexpected dylibs compared to historical baselines

data_components.name: Process Creation
data_components.channel: execution of process with DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES set

mutable_elements.description: macOS linker variables like DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES. Tunable to development environments where use may be expected.
Known dylibs typically loaded by apps. Deviations highlight potential hijacking.
Locations where dylibs are monitored for tampering (e.g., /Applications, /System/Library, /tmp).

T1574.007.name: Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Hijack Execution Flow using Path Interception by PATH Environment Variable.

analytics.name: Analytic 0009
analytics.description: Abnormal modification of the PATH environment variable or registry keys controlling system paths, combined with execution of binaries named after legitimate system tools from user-writable directories. Defender correlates registry modifications, file creation of suspicious binaries, and process execution paths inconsistent with baseline system directories.

mutable_elements.description: PATH environment keys under HKCU and HKLM to monitor for changes.
List of high-value system binaries commonly hijacked (e.g., net.exe, python.exe, powershell.exe).
Correlation window between PATH modification and execution of a hijacked binary.

analytics.name: Analytic 0010
analytics.description: User modification of the $PATH environment variable in shell configuration files or direct runtime PATH changes, followed by execution of binaries from user-controlled directories. Defender observes file edits to ~/.bashrc, ~/.profile, or /etc/paths.d and process execution resolving to unexpected binary locations.

data_components.name: Process Creation
data_components.channel: Execution of binary resolved from $PATH not located in /usr/bin or /bin

mutable_elements.description: Set of shell startup files where PATH changes should be flagged.
Directories (e.g., /usr/local/bin) considered safe to avoid FP.

analytics.name: Analytic 0011
analytics.description: Modification of PATH or HOME environment variables through shell config files, launchctl, or /etc/paths.d entries, combined with process execution from attacker-controlled directories. Defender correlates file changes in /etc/paths.d with process execution resolving to malicious binaries.

data_components.name: Process Creation
data_components.channel: Process execution path inconsistent with baseline PATH directories

data_components.name: File Modification
data_components.channel: File modification in /etc/paths.d or user shell rc files

mutable_elements.description: Monitor /etc/paths.d and $HOME for unauthorized entries.
Baseline applications expected in user PATH directories.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Hijack Execution Flow using Path Interception by Search Order Hijacking

analytics.name: Analytic 1560
analytics.description: Processes executing binaries named after legitimate system utilities (e.g., net.exe, findstr.exe, python.exe) from non-standard or application-specific directories, combined with file creation or modification events for such binaries. Defender correlates file writes in vulnerable directories, process execution paths inconsistent with baseline system paths, and abnormal parent-child relationships in process lineage.

mutable_elements.description: Common system utilities often hijacked (e.g., net.exe, cmd.exe, powershell.exe, python.exe).
Directories where executables should not normally be written (e.g., application folders, user profile subdirs).
Correlation window between file creation and subsequent process execution.
Expected parent processes for critical system binaries, deviations may indicate hijacking.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Hijack Execution Flow through Path Interception by Unquoted Path

analytics.name: Analytic 0176
analytics.description: Unquoted service or shortcut paths that contain spaces and allow path interception by higher-level executables. Defender observes registry service configurations with unquoted paths, file creation of executables in parent directories of unquoted paths, and subsequent process execution from unexpected locations.

mutable_elements.description: List of critical services to check for unquoted paths in ImagePath registry keys.
Executables with names matching potential interception targets (e.g., program.exe, net.exe).
Correlation interval between file creation in parent directories and execution of unquoted path process.
Known good service paths for comparison against modified or unquoted values.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Hijack Execution Flow through Services File Permissions Weakness.

analytics.name: Analytic 1211
analytics.description: Modification or replacement of service executables due to weak file or directory permissions. Defender observes file writes to service binary paths, unexpected modifications of executables associated with registered services, and subsequent service execution of attacker-supplied binaries under elevated permissions.

mutable_elements.description: List of critical services and their expected executable paths for integrity checking.
Baseline hashes of legitimate service executables for tamper detection.
Correlation interval between file modification of service executables and service execution.
Accounts allowed to legitimately modify service executables.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Hijack Execution Flow through Service Registry Premission Weakness.

analytics.name: Analytic 1195
analytics.description: Unauthorized modification of service-related registry keys such as ImagePath, FailureCommand, ServiceDll, or Performance/Parameters keys. Defender correlates registry modifications, anomalous service metadata changes, and subsequent service process executions that deviate from baseline configurations.

mutable_elements.description: Registry subkeys for critical services (ImagePath, ServiceDll, FailureCommand, Parameters).
Known good service registry configurations and paths for comparison.
Correlation interval between registry/service modifications and service execution.
Accounts permitted to modify service configurations.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Hijack Execution Flow using the Windows COR_PROFILER.

analytics.name: Analytic 1319
analytics.description: Modification of COR_PROFILER-related environment variables or Registry keys (COR_ENABLE_PROFILING, COR_PROFILER, COR_PROFILER_PATH), combined with anomalous .NET process creation or unmanaged DLL loads. Defender observes registry modifications, suspicious process creation with altered environment variables, and profiler DLLs loaded unexpectedly into .NET CLR processes.

mutable_elements.description: List of known good COR_PROFILER CLSIDs and DLLs expected in developer or monitoring environments.
Processes expected to load COR_PROFILER (e.g., Visual Studio) for baseline comparison.
Interval between registry modification or file creation and profiler DLL load into .NET processes.
Directories considered legitimate for profiler DLLs; deviations should raise alerts.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Hijack Execution Flow through the KernelCallbackTable on Windows.

analytics.name: Analytic 1593
analytics.description: Unexpected modification of the KernelCallbackTable in a process’s PEB followed by invocation of modified callback functions (e.g., fnCOPYDATA) through Windows messages. Defender observes suspicious API call chains such as NtQueryInformationProcess → WriteProcessMemory → abnormal GUI callback execution, often correlating to anomalous process behavior such as network activity or code injection.

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: WriteProcessMemory: WriteProcessMemory targeting regions containing KernelCallbackTable addresses

mutable_elements.description: GUI applications (e.g., explorer.exe, notepad.exe) where KernelCallbackTable abuse is more likely.
Specific callback functions (e.g., fnCOPYDATA, fnDWORD) expected to remain stable.
Correlation interval between WriteProcessMemory calls and execution of modified callback functions.
Access rights values that should be flagged when targeting GUI processes.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Hijack Execution Flow through the AppDomainManager on Windows.

analytics.name: Analytic 1433
analytics.description: Detection focuses on unauthorized manipulation of .NET AppDomainManager behavior. Defenders may observe suspicious creation of new AppDomains within trusted processes, anomalous loading of assemblies via non-standard configuration files, or registry/environment variable changes redirecting AppDomainManager to malicious assemblies. Correlated events include config file tampering, new process creation of .NET host processes (e.g., w3wp.exe, powershell.exe) with modified runtime parameters, and module loads of unusual or unsigned .NET DLLs.

mutable_elements.description: List of monitored .NET host processes (e.g., powershell.exe, w3wp.exe, svchost.exe).
Known benign .NET assemblies expected to load via AppDomainManager.
Directory paths where configuration tampering should be monitored (application directories, system32, program files).
Correlation period between file modification of config/environment settings and subsequent anomalous module load.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure

analytics.name: Analytic 0861
analytics.description: Detection focuses on identifying unauthorized or anomalous changes to compute infrastructure components. Defender perspective: monitor for creation, deletion, or modification of instances, volumes, and snapshots outside of approved change management windows; correlate abnormal activity such as rapid snapshot creation followed by new instance mounts, or repeated infrastructure changes by rarely used accounts. Flagging activity linked to unusual geolocation, API client, or automation script is suspicious.

data_components.name: Cloud Service Metadata
data_components.channel: unexpected IAM user or role assuming privileges for instance/snapshot operations

mutable_elements.description: Approved maintenance or deployment windows. Helps reduce false positives by distinguishing scheduled activity.
IAM user, role, or service account performing the operation. Tunable to allowlist known automation services.
Number of infrastructure changes (e.g., snapshot creations) in a defined period. Adjusted based on workload scale.
Region or source IP where changes originate. Useful for tuning alerts to account for multi-region deployments.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Create Snapshot

analytics.name: Analytic 1187
analytics.description: Detection focuses on correlating snapshot creation events with subsequent instance creation and mounting activities. From a defender perspective, suspicious sequences include snapshot creation by unexpected or newly created IAM users, snapshots created from sensitive volumes without preceding change-control activity, or snapshots immediately followed by mounting to unauthorized instances. Cross-referencing with user behavior, IP geolocation, and automation context helps distinguish benign backup operations from adversary-driven snapshot exploitation.

mutable_elements.description: IAM user, service account, or role performing snapshot creation. Tuned to allowlist known backup automation services.
Frequency of snapshot creation in a defined period. Adjusted for environments with frequent automated backups.
Unusual regions or IPs from which snapshot creation API calls originate. Helps identify cross-region snapshot abuse.
Tagging or classification of volumes being snapshotted. Tuned to prioritize alerts when sensitive volumes are copied.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Create Cloud Instance

analytics.name: Analytic 1242
analytics.description: Detection focuses on abnormal or unauthorized cloud instance creation events. From a defender’s perspective, suspicious behavior includes VM/instance creation by rarely used or newly created accounts, creation events from unusual geolocations, or rapid sequences of snapshot creation followed by instance creation and mounting. Unexpected network or IAM policy changes applied to new instances can indicate adversarial use rather than legitimate provisioning.

mutable_elements.description: IAM user, service account, or role creating the instance. Tuned to allowlist known automation services.
Region or source IP where the creation request originates. Helps detect cross-region or unusual location abuse.
Number of instances created per user or account in a time window. Tuned for environments with elastic scaling.
Expected tags (e.g., owner, purpose, cost center) for new instances. Deviations may indicate adversarial creation.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Delete Cloud Instance

analytics.name: Analytic 0234
analytics.description: Defenders can detect suspicious cloud instance deletions by correlating events across authentication, instance lifecycle, and account activity. From a defender’s perspective, behaviors of interest include instances deleted shortly after creation, deletions initiated by new or rarely used accounts, deletions following snapshot creation, and deletions originating from anomalous geolocations or access keys. These may indicate adversarial attempts to destroy forensic evidence or evade detection.

mutable_elements.description: Identity of the user/service account performing deletions; tuned to exclude automation or known administrative workflows.
Threshold for detecting rapid instance lifecycle events (e.g., creation and deletion within minutes).
Region or source IP where the delete request originated; can be tuned to align with enterprise cloud geography.
Number of deletions per user/account in a defined window; tuned for organizations with high elasticity.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Revert Cloud Instance

analytics.name: Analytic 0953
analytics.description: Defenders can detect suspicious reversion of cloud compute instances by monitoring for unusual snapshot restores, rollback actions, or ephemeral storage resets that occur outside expected administrative workflows. From a defender’s perspective, relevant detection chains include: a snapshot restore triggered by a new or rarely used account, a sequence of snapshot creation immediately followed by a restore and instance start, or rollbacks performed from anomalous geographic or network locations. These patterns may indicate attempts to remove forensic evidence or re-establish a clean execution state for persistence.

mutable_elements.description: Identity of the user or service account performing rollback actions; tuned to exclude automation or approved workflows.
Threshold for correlating snapshot creation followed by reversion within minutes; tuned to environment activity norms.
Region or source IP where the revert request originated; tuned to align with enterprise cloud geography.
Use of administrative tags or headers to distinguish legitimate restores from malicious activity.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Modify Cloud Compute Infrastructure: Modify Cloud Compute Configurations

analytics.name: Analytic 1356
analytics.description: Defenders should monitor for anomalous or unauthorized changes to cloud compute configurations that alter quotas, tenant-wide policies, subscription associations, or allowed deployment regions. From a defender’s perspective, suspicious behavior chains include a sudden increase in compute quota requests followed by new instance or resource creation, policy modifications that weaken security restrictions, or enabling previously unused/unsupported cloud regions. Correlation across identity, configuration, and subsequent provisioning logs is critical to distinguish legitimate administrative activity from adversarial abuse.

mutable_elements.description: Identity performing the quota or configuration change; tuned to filter known admins or automation accounts.
Correlation period for configuration change followed by resource creation; tuned to environment norms.
Type of configuration being modified (quota, policy, region); tuned to organization-specific risk thresholds.
Region where the configuration change originates; tuned to enterprise’s expected operational geography.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Cloud Infrastructure Discovery

analytics.name: Analytic 0481
analytics.description: Defenders should monitor for suspicious enumeration of cloud infrastructure components via APIs or CLI tools. Observable behaviors include repeated listing or description operations for compute instances, snapshots, storage buckets, and volumes. From a defender’s perspective, risky activity is often identified by new or untrusted identities making discovery calls (e.g., DescribeInstances, ListBuckets, az vm list, gcloud compute instances list), enumeration from unusual geolocations or IPs, or rapid multi-service discovery in sequence. Correlating discovery API usage with later snapshot creation or instance modification provides further context of adversary behavior.

mutable_elements.description: Identity performing the discovery operation; tuned to filter known administrative or inventory accounts.
Source region or IP of discovery requests; tuned to expected operational regions to detect unusual access.
Correlation period to link enumeration calls with subsequent provisioning or exfiltration activity.
Rate or volume of discovery calls; tuned to suppress noise from inventory management tools.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Network Boundary Bridging

analytics.name: Analytic 0015
analytics.description: From a defender’s perspective, suspicious bridging is observed when network devices begin allowing traffic that contradicts existing segmentation or access policies. Observable behaviors include sudden modifications to ACLs or firewall rules, unusual cross-boundary traffic flows (e.g., east-west communications across separated VLANs), or simultaneous ingress/egress anomalies. Multi-event correlation is key: configuration changes on a router/firewall followed by unexpected traffic patterns, especially from unusual sources, is a strong indicator of compromise.

data_components.name: Network Traffic Flow
data_components.channel: Unexpected flows between segmented networks or prohibited ports

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: ACL/Firewall rule modification or new route injection

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window between configuration changes and abnormal traffic; tuned to match expected administrative change cycles.
Known authorized ACL/firewall changes; suppresses noise from legitimate maintenance.
Geographic origin of new traffic patterns; helps distinguish benign remote offices from suspicious foreign access.
Volume of cross-segment traffic; tuned to detect large-scale lateral flows without flagging small test connections.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Network Address Translation Traversal

analytics.name: Analytic 0465
analytics.description: Defenders may observe unauthorized or anomalous changes to NAT configurations, including the addition of new translation rules or modifications to existing ones. Suspicious behaviors include sudden introduction of NAT mappings bridging segmented networks, new port address translation rules that obscure true source IPs, or traffic flows inconsistent with expected network design. Multi-event correlation includes detecting configuration changes on routers/firewalls, followed by traffic traversing unexpected internal/external address pairs.

data_components.name: Network Traffic Flow
data_components.channel: Source/destination IP translation inconsistent with intended policy

mutable_elements.description: Time correlation window between NAT rule change and unexpected traffic; adjustable to align with change management practices.
Whitelist of approved NAT policies and rules; prevents false positives from legitimate operations.
Threshold for abnormal traffic across NAT; tuned to differentiate testing from large-scale exfiltration or bridging.
Specific interfaces or zones monitored for NAT translation; allows tuning for internal vs. external-facing boundaries.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Weaken Encryption on Network Devices

analytics.name: Analytic 0961
analytics.description: Defenders may observe unauthorized modifications to encryption-related configuration files, firmware, or crypto modules on network devices. Suspicious patterns include changes to cipher suite configurations, unexpected firmware updates affecting crypto libraries, disabling of hardware cryptographic accelerators, or reductions in key length policies. Correlating configuration changes with anomalies in encrypted traffic characteristics (e.g., weaker ciphers or sudden plaintext transmission) strengthens detection.

data_components.name: Module Load
data_components.channel: Status change in cryptographic hardware modules (enabled -> disabled)

data_components.name: File Modification
data_components.channel: Configuration change events referencing encryption, TLS/SSL, or IPSec settings

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: Traffic patterns showing downgrade from strong encryption (AES-256) to weaker or plaintext protocols

mutable_elements.description: List of approved encryption algorithms and key lengths; customizable to organizational policy.
Correlation period between configuration changes and abnormal traffic; adjustable to reduce false positives.
Known trusted sources of firmware updates; deviations indicate possible compromise.
Baseline entropy measurements of encrypted traffic; deviations may reveal weakening of encryption.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Weaken Encryption: Reduce Key Space on Network Devices

analytics.name: Analytic 0681
analytics.description: Defenders may observe attempts to alter cryptographic settings on network devices that reduce key strength or allowable cipher suites. Suspicious indicators include configuration changes that downgrade encryption algorithms, key length parameters, or the disabling of strong encryption in favor of legacy ciphers. These activities often appear as CLI commands modifying crypto policies, firmware changes affecting crypto libraries, or unexpected updates to key management files. Correlation across device config logs and traffic analysis showing weaker ciphers provides higher confidence of malicious key space reduction.

data_components.name: File Modification
data_components.channel: Configuration changes referencing 'crypto', 'key length', 'cipher', or downgrade of encryption settings

data_components.name: Command Execution
data_components.channel: Execution of CLI commands altering crypto parameters (e.g., 'crypto key generate rsa modulus 512')

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: Observed downgrade in negotiated cipher suites or TLS/SSH versions across sessions

mutable_elements.description: Defines the minimum acceptable encryption key sizes; tunable to organizational policy.
Baseline list of approved cipher suites for network sessions; deviations may indicate tampering.
Whitelisted accounts for executing crypto configuration changes; ensures alerts only trigger on unauthorized actions.
Time correlation period between configuration change and anomalous traffic downgrade; adjustable to reduce noise.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Weaken Encryption: Disable Crypto Hardware on Network Devices

analytics.name: Analytic 1360
analytics.description: Defenders may observe attempts to disable dedicated crypto hardware on network devices, often visible through anomalous CLI commands, unexpected firmware or configuration updates, and degraded encryption performance. Suspicious indicators include commands that alter hardware acceleration settings (e.g., disabling AES-NI or crypto engines), modification of system image files, or logs showing fallback from hardware to software encryption. Network traffic analysis may also reveal a sudden downgrade in throughput or cipher negotiation behavior consistent with the absence of hardware acceleration.

data_components.name: File Modification
data_components.channel: Configuration changes referencing cryptographic hardware modules or disabling hardware acceleration

data_components.name: Command Execution
data_components.channel: Execution of commands disabling crypto hardware acceleration (e.g., 'no crypto engine enable')

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: Degraded encryption throughput or switch to weaker cipher suites compared to historical baselines

mutable_elements.description: Defines trusted administrator accounts allowed to modify encryption hardware settings; deviations trigger alerts.
Expected performance metrics with hardware acceleration enabled; drops may indicate tampering.
Whitelist of vendor-signed firmware versions; unexpected updates could signal malicious modification.
Period of correlation between configuration change and observed traffic downgrade; tunable to reduce false positives.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Modify System Image on Network Devices

analytics.name: Analytic 0482
analytics.description: Defenders may observe adversary attempts to alter or replace a network device’s operating system image through anomalous CLI commands, unexpected firmware updates, integrity check failures, or mismatches in version and checksum validation. Suspicious behavior includes modification of image files on storage, OS version output inconsistent with baselines, unexpected reloads or reboots after image replacement, and changes to boot configuration that load non-standard system images.

data_components.name: File Modification
data_components.channel: Configuration changes to boot variables, startup image paths, or checksum verification failures

data_components.name: Command Execution
data_components.channel: Execution of commands to load, copy, or replace system images (e.g., 'copy tftp flash', 'boot system')

mutable_elements.description: Defines trusted administrator accounts allowed to modify system images; deviations indicate possible malicious modification.
Whitelist of validated vendor OS images; unexpected versions may suggest adversarial tampering.
Correlation window for detecting config changes followed by firmware updates or reboots.
Baseline cryptographic hashes of approved system images; deviations may indicate compromise.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Patch System Image on Network Devices

analytics.name: Analytic 1293
analytics.description: Defenders may observe adversary attempts to patch system images by monitoring for anomalous file transfers (TFTP, SCP, FTP) of image files, unauthorized CLI commands altering boot system variables, integrity check mismatches between running and baseline OS images, and runtime memory manipulation attempts. Suspicious sequences include uploading a new image, modifying boot parameters, and subsequent reload/reboot of the device. In-memory patching attempts may manifest as debug commands or boot loader manipulation inconsistent with normal administrative activity.

data_components.name: Firmware Modification
data_components.channel: Debug or memory access commands indicating attempts to alter OS instructions in memory

data_components.name: File Modification
data_components.channel: Configuration changes to startup image paths, boot loader parameters, or debug flags

data_components.name: Command Execution
data_components.channel: Execution of privileged commands such as 'copy tftp flash', 'boot system', or 'debug memory'

mutable_elements.description: Whitelist of validated vendor OS versions; deviations may indicate tampering.
Trusted admin accounts permitted to update images; anomalies suggest compromise.
Baseline hash of approved images; used for detecting file tampering.
Correlation period for detecting chained behaviors (file upload → boot config change → reboot).

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Downgrade System Image on Network Devices

analytics.name: Analytic 1570
analytics.description: Defenders may observe adversary attempts to downgrade system images by monitoring for anomalous file transfers of OS image files (via TFTP, FTP, SCP), configuration changes pointing boot system variables to older image files, unexpected OS version strings after reboot, and checksum mismatches against approved baseline images. Suspicious chains include transfer of an older image, alteration of boot configuration, and reboot/reload of the device. Adversaries may also tamper with CLI output to disguise downgrade attempts, requiring independent validation of OS version and integrity.

data_components.name: File Metadata
data_components.channel: OS version query results inconsistent with expected or approved version list

data_components.name: File Modification
data_components.channel: Configuration changes referencing older image versions or unexpected boot parameters

data_components.name: Command Execution
data_components.channel: Execution of commands such as 'copy tftp flash', 'boot system <image>', 'reload'

mutable_elements.description: Whitelist of supported and validated OS versions for devices; helps reduce false positives.
Baseline cryptographic hashes of valid OS images; deviations indicate possible downgrade or tampering.
Correlation period to detect the chain of file transfer → boot config change → reboot event.
Accounts authorized to perform OS upgrades/downgrades; anomalies suggest misuse or compromise.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Data from Configuration Repository on Network Devices

analytics.name: Analytic 1630
analytics.description: Defenders may observe adversary attempts to extract configuration data from management repositories by monitoring for anomalous SNMP queries, API calls, or protocol requests (e.g., NETCONF, RESTCONF) that enumerate system configuration. Suspicious sequences include repeated queries from untrusted IPs, abnormal query types requesting sensitive configuration data, or repository access occurring outside of normal administrative maintenance windows. Abnormal authentication attempts, sudden enumeration of device inventory, or bulk data transfer of configuration files may also be observed.

data_components.name: Network Connection Creation
data_components.channel: Unexpected or unauthorized inbound connections to SNMP, NETCONF, or RESTCONF services

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: Authentication failures or unusual community string usage in SNMP queries

mutable_elements.description: Expected IP ranges or hosts permitted to query configuration repositories; deviations may indicate compromise.
Time periods when configuration queries normally occur; anomalies outside these windows may be suspicious.
Number of queries allowed within a given period before an anomaly is triggered.
Expected usage of SNMP, NETCONF, or RESTCONF; deviations from baseline patterns may indicate misuse.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for SNMP (MIB Dump) on Network Devices

analytics.name: Analytic 1249
analytics.description: Defenders may observe suspicious SNMP MIB enumeration through abnormal queries for large sets of OIDs, repeated SNMP GETBULK/GETNEXT requests, or queries originating from non-administrative IP addresses. Anomalous use of community strings, authentication failures, or enumeration activity outside maintenance windows may also indicate attempts to dump MIB contents. Correlation across syslog, NetFlow, and SNMP audit data can reveal chains of behavior such as repeated authentication failures followed by successful large-scale OID retrieval.

data_components.name: File Modification
data_components.channel: SNMP configuration changes, such as enabling read/write access or modifying community strings

data_components.name: Network Connection Creation
data_components.channel: High-volume or repeated SNMP GETBULK/GETNEXT queries from untrusted or external IPs

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: Authentication failures, unexpected community string usage, or unauthorized SNMPv1/v2 requests

mutable_elements.description: Expected IP ranges allowed to query SNMP. Deviation indicates possible misuse.
Baseline frequency and volume of SNMP queries; anomalies above threshold may indicate dumping.
Expected community strings (e.g., hashed or custom values). Unrecognized strings may signal abuse.
Time periods during which SNMP queries are authorized. Queries outside these hours may be malicious.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Network Device Configuration Dump via Config Repositories

analytics.name: Analytic 0647
analytics.description: Defenders may observe adversary attempts to collect or export full device configurations by detecting unusual SNMP queries, Smart Install (SMI) activity, or CLI/API commands that request running or startup configuration dumps. Correlated behaviors include high-volume read requests for sensitive OIDs, repeated use of 'show running-config' or equivalent commands from untrusted IPs, or unexpected TFTP/SCP/FTP transfers containing configuration files. These behaviors often appear in sequence: anomalous authentication or privilege escalation, followed by bulk configuration retrieval and outbound transfer.

data_components.name: Command Execution
data_components.channel: Execution of commands like 'show running-config', 'copy running-config', or 'export config'

data_components.name: Network Connection Creation
data_components.channel: GETBULK/GETNEXT requests for OIDs associated with configuration parameters

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: Outbound SCP, TFTP, or FTP sessions carrying configuration file content

mutable_elements.description: Known trusted IP addresses permitted to execute configuration dump commands.
Baseline frequency of legitimate configuration exports; anomalies above threshold may indicate malicious activity.
Expected transfer methods (e.g., SCP vs. TFTP). Unexpected use of weak protocols may indicate exfiltration.
Normal maintenance windows for authorized configuration exports; activity outside these windows may be suspicious.

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Forged Web Credentials

analytics.name: Analytic 0717
analytics.description: Defenders may detect adversaries forging web credentials in IaaS environments by monitoring for anomalous API activity such as AssumeRole or GetFederationToken being executed by unusual principals. These events often correlate with sudden logon sessions from unfamiliar IP addresses or regions. The chain is usually secret material misuse (stolen private key or password) → API request generating a new token → access to high-value resources.

data_components.channel: AssumeRole, GetFederationToken API calls by unusual or new entities

data_components.name: Logon Session Creation
data_components.channel: Temporary security credentials used to authenticate into management console or APIs

mutable_elements.description: Define expected users and roles allowed to use AssumeRole or federation APIs.
Alert if the same user authenticates from geographically disparate locations within a short time.

analytics.name: Analytic 0718
analytics.description: Forged web credentials may manifest as anomalous SAML token issuance, OpenID Connect token minting, or Zimbra pre-auth key usage. Defenders may see tokens issued without normal authentication events, multiple valid tokens generated simultaneously, or signing anomalies in IdP logs.

data_components.name: Web Credential Usage
data_components.channel: Pre-authentication keys generated or token signing anomalies

Define normal authentication flows (e.g., password+MFA) to baseline token issuance.

analytics.name: Analytic 0719
analytics.description: Forged web credentials on Windows endpoints may be detected by anomalous browser cookie files, local token cache manipulations, or tools injecting tokens into sessions. Defenders may observe processes accessing LSASS or browser credential stores unexpectedly, followed by unusual logon sessions.

analytics.name: Analytic 0720
analytics.description: On Linux systems, forged credentials may be injected into browser session files, curl/wget headers, or token caches in memory. Detection can leverage auditd to track processes accessing sensitive files (~/.mozilla, ~/.config/chromium, ~/.aws/credentials) and correlate with suspicious outbound connections.

analytics.name: Analytic 0721
analytics.description: Forged credentials on macOS may be visible through Unified Logs showing abnormal access to Keychain or browser session files. Correlated with anomalous web session usage from Safari or Chrome processes outside typical user context.

data_components.channel: Web sessions initiated with newly forged tokens

data_components.name: Logon Session Creation
data_components.channel: Access to Keychain items or browser credential stores

mutable_elements.description: List applications that normally request Keychain credentials.

analytics.name: Analytic 0722
analytics.description: SaaS platforms may show forged credentials as unusual API keys, tokens, or session cookies being used without corresponding authentication. Correlated patterns include simultaneous valid sessions from multiple geographies, unusual API calls with new tokens, or bypass of expected MFA enforcement.

data_components.name: Web Credential Creation
data_components.channel: Session creation without MFA or login event

data_components.name: Web Credential Usage
data_components.channel: API requests made with tokens not associated with expected user logins

mutable_elements.description: Trigger on logins from unusual or high-risk geographies.
Detect multiple simultaneous uses of the same forged credential.

analytics.name: Analytic 0723
analytics.description: Forged web credentials in Office Suite contexts may appear as abnormal authentication headers in Outlook or Teams traffic, or unexplained OAuth grants in M365/Azure logs. Defenders should correlate token usage events with missing authentication flows and mismatched device/user context.

data_components.name: Logon Session Creation
data_components.channel: Token usage events with device/user mismatch

strategies.name: Detection Strategy for Forged Web Cookies

analytics.name: Analytic 0483
analytics.description: Forged cookies in IaaS environments may appear as authentication attempts that bypass MFA, leveraging AssumeRole or session APIs with cookies that were never legitimately issued. strategies.name: Detection of Stage Capabilities

analytics.name: Analytic 1971
analytics.description:
If infrastructure or patterns in malware, tooling, certificates, or malicious web content have been previously identified, internet scanning may uncover when an adversary has staged their capabilities.
Much of this activity will take place outside the visibility of the target organization, making detection of this behavior difficult. Detection efforts may be focused on related stages of the adversary lifecycle, such as initial access and post-compromise behaviors.

strategies.name: Detection of Upload Malware

analytics.name: Analytic 1956
analytics.description:
If infrastructure or patterns in malware have been previously identified, internet scanning may uncover when an adversary has staged malware to make it accessible for targeting.
Much of this activity will take place outside the visibility of the target organization, making detection of this behavior difficult. Detection efforts may be focused on post-compromise phases of the adversary lifecycle, such as [User Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204) or [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105) .

strategies.name: Detection of Upload Tool

analytics.name: Analytic 1966
analytics.description:
If infrastructure or patterns in tooling have been previously identified, internet scanning may uncover when an adversary has staged tools to make them accessible for targeting.
Much of this activity will take place outside the visibility of the target organization, making detection of this behavior difficult. Detection efforts may be focused on post-compromise phases of the adversary lifecycle, such as [Ingress Tool Transfer](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1105).

strategies.name: Detection of Install Digital Certificate

analytics.name: Analytic 1972
analytics.description:
Consider use of services that may aid in the tracking of certificates in use on sites across the Internet. In some cases it may be possible to pivot on known pieces of certificate information to uncover other adversary infrastructure.(Citation: Splunk Kovar Certificates 2017)
Detection efforts may be focused on related behaviors, such as [Web Protocols](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001) or [Asymmetric Cryptography](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1573/002).

strategies.name: Detection of Drive-by Target

analytics.name: Analytic 1957
analytics.description:
If infrastructure or patterns in the malicious web content utilized to deliver a [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) have been previously identified, internet scanning may uncover when an adversary has staged web content for use in a strategic web compromise.
Much of this activity will take place outside the visibility of the target organization, making detection of this behavior difficult. Detection efforts may be focused on other phases of the adversary lifecycle, such as [Drive-by Compromise](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1189) or [Exploitation for Client Execution](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1203).

strategies.name: Detection of Link Target

analytics.name: Analytic 2025
analytics.description:
If infrastructure or patterns in malicious web content have been previously identified, internet scanning may uncover when an adversary has staged web content to make it accessible for targeting.
