Enterprise-specific allow list of packages expected to register BOOT_COMPLETED receivers.
OEM- and ROM-specific list of system and vendor init script locations that should be immutable in production devices.
Expected Verified Boot, SafetyNet, and OEM attestation states for enrolled devices. Custom ROM or dev devices may need relaxed thresholds.
Number or rate of attestation failures before escalating to a high-severity incident.

analytics.name: Analytic 1740
analytics.description: Correlates unauthorized alterations to launchd configuration (LaunchDaemons/LaunchAgents plists), background execution entitlements, or sideloaded app containers with suspicious auto-start behavior during device boot or user unlock. From the defender’s view this shows up as new or modified plist files in launchd directories, launchd starting binaries from non-Apple or non-AppStore locations, and apps with unexpected background modes that remain active immediately after boot/unlock.

data_components.name: Process Creation
data_components.channel: launchd invocation of binary from non-Apple, non-AppStore, or sideloaded location during boot or shortly after unlock

data_components.name: File Modification
data_components.channel: Creation or modification of LaunchDaemon or LaunchAgent plist in /System/Library/LaunchDaemons, /Library/LaunchDaemons, or /Library/LaunchAgents

data_components.name: Application Assets
data_components.channel: Application gaining or using unexpected background execution entitlements or modes

mutable_elements.description: List of filesystem paths or process names that identify intentionally jailbroken lab devices and should be handled differently.
Organization-specific list of allowed launchd job labels and binary paths.
Per-app allow list for background execution modes (for example, VOIP, location) to reduce noise.
Time window after boot or unlock within which unexpected launchd auto-starts are considered high risk.

strategies.name: Detection of Exploitation for Privilege Escalation

analytics.name: Analytic 1758
analytics.description:
From the defender’s perspective, this strategy correlates signals that a previously unprivileged Android app or process has gained higher privileges through exploitation rather than normal OS or MDM flows. 
Observable behaviors include: 
(1) unprivileged app processes issuing sensitive syscalls or accessing privileged device interfaces, 
(2) bursts of SELinux denials followed by an unexpected domain or permission change, 
(3) creation of new processes running with system or root UID whose lineage traces back to an app sandbox path, and 
(4) crashes or abnormal restarts of privileged system services followed shortly by a new connection or binder interaction from the same low-privileged app. The focus is on unusual privilege transitions, anomalous process ancestry, and OS security policy violations, not on specific exploit binaries or CVE signatures.

data_components.name: Host Status
data_components.channel: Crash or abnormal restart of privileged system services (for example, system_server, mediaserver, installd) followed shortly by new privileged process activity or binder connections from a single app UID

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: Unprivileged app process (app UID, non-system) invoking sensitive syscalls or device interfaces associated with privilege escalation (setuid, ptrace, perf_event_open, vulnerable drivers)

data_components.name: Process Creation
data_components.channel: Creation of a new process running as system or root UID whose executable path resides under an app container path (for example, /data/app or /data/user/0/<pkg>), or whose parent process originates from an app sandbox

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window (for example, 60–300 seconds) between SELinux events, crashes, and privilege changes to reduce noise while still capturing exploit chains.
UID ranges that represent unprivileged application accounts in a specific Android OEM or enterprise deployment.
List of syscalls considered indicative of privilege escalation attempts; may vary by kernel version, OEM drivers, and threat model.
Set of high-value Android system services where crashes or restarts are particularly suspicious (for example, system_server, mediaserver).
Enterprise-defined mapping of UIDs considered elevated (for example, root, system, radio) for alert scoping.

analytics.name: Analytic 1759
analytics.description: Correlates app sandbox escape attempts via unsigned binary execution, mmap memory permission changes (RWX), and sandbox profile violations. Detection chain includes app leveraging JIT/JSC to execute shellcode or triggering kernel exploit via crafted IOKit or Mach port abuse.

data_components.name: Host Status
data_components.channel: code signature validation failure / exec of invalidly-signed payload from sandboxed app

data_components.name: API Calls
data_components.channel: mmap with PROT_EXEC and PROT_WRITE by sandboxed app

mutable_elements.description: Allowlist known benign unsigned binaries for reducing FP.
Adjustable threshold for RWX page allocation frequency or size.
May require tuning based on OS version and legitimate app usage (e.g., Safari JIT).

strategies.name: Detection of Obfuscated Files or Information

analytics.name: Analytic 1851
analytics.description: Defender correlates a sandboxed app writing high-entropy or encoded artifacts (often in app-private or shared storage), performing decode/decompress/reassembly, then dynamically loading/execing the resulting code (DexClassLoader/JNI dlopen) or spawning a helper process. Sequence: high-entropy file writes → decode/unpack bursts → new .dex/.so/.jar creation in temp/obfuscated paths → dynamic load or shell spawn within a tight window.

data_components.name: Module Load
data_components.channel: DexClassLoader/PathClassLoader load attempt from non-standard path or recently created file

data_components.name: Module Load
data_components.channel: Short burst of file I/O followed by JNI/dlopen of a newly created .so

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: App UID writes new file with suspicious extension/location (.tmp, .dat, .enc, /data/data/<pkg>/files/, /sdcard/Download/) and high estimated entropy

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: TLS/HTTP download with atypical MIME (application/octet-stream, application/x-zip, application/x-gzip) followed by local decode/write

data_components.name: API Calls
data_components.channel: SELinux AVC related to execute_no_trans/execmem after decode/unpack activity by the same app UID

mutable_elements.description: Max interval to correlate write→decode→load stages (e.g., 5–60s depending on device performance).
Shannon entropy threshold to flag likely obfuscated blobs (e.g., ≥ 7.2).
Directories to monitor (e.g., app /files, cache, /sdcard/Download). OEMs vary.
Minimum count of small sequential writes (split payload reassembly).
Benign CDNs/hosts for large opaque downloads to reduce FPs.
Regex for newly loaded .dex/.so/.jar/temp artifacts.
Foreground/background or developer mode context to suppress test noise.

analytics.name: Analytic 1852
analytics.description: Defender correlates a sandboxed app downloading or receiving opaque/encoded blobs, writing high-entropy content into container/tmp, performing decode/decompress/reassembly, and then executing/loaded as Mach-O or bundle (dlopen) or leveraging JIT/RWX pages to run the decoded payload. Sequence: opaque download or IPC → high-entropy writes/split-file bursts → decode/unarchive → new Mach-O/bundle in tmp → dlopen/posix_spawn or RWX region activity.

data_components.name: Module Load
data_components.channel: dyld: dlopen/dyld_cache load from non-standard app-writable path

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: mmap/mprotect transitions to PROT_EXEC for pages associated with recently written files

data_components.name: Process Access
data_components.channel: Code signing validation events referencing newly written local Mach-O/bundle prior to exec or dlopen

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: NSFileHandle/NSFileManager writes creating high-entropy files within app container (/var/mobile/Containers/Data/Application/<GUID>/tmp|Library/Caches)

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: Per-app VPN flow logging indicating opaque/archived payload transfer preceding local decode

mutable_elements.description: Max interval to link write→decode→load/exec (e.g., 5–45s depending on device and iOS version).
Entropy threshold to consider a file obfuscated/packed (e.g., ≥ 7.3).
Minimum count of small sequential writes to flag reassembly behaviors.
Container subpaths to monitor (tmp, Library/Caches, Documents) vary by policy.
Allowlist of legitimate dynamically loaded bundles/plugins to reduce FPs.
Known enterprise services carrying opaque archives to avoid false alerts.

strategies.name: Detection of Steganography

analytics.name: Analytic 1780
analytics.description: Defender correlates an app's opaque media ingress (download/IPC) with high-entropy or anomalous edits to image/audio/video files in app-writable storage (e.g., bursts of bitmap/codec operations, EXIF/IPTC/XMP mutation, suspicious container growth), followed by decoding/extraction behavior (new non-media artifact derived from the edited media) and optional exfiltration/sharing of the stego media. Focus is on: (1) opaque media arrival → (2) rapid metadata or pixel-domain mutations with atypical size/entropy deltas → (3a) decoded payload creation or dynamic load from decoded path, and/or (3b) upload/share of the modified media within a tight window.

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: App UID writes edited media to container paths (e.g., /data/data/<pkg>/files/, .../cache/, /storage/emulated/0/Pictures/<pkg>/) with high delta in size vs. original and elevated estimated segment entropy

data_components.name: File Modification
data_components.channel: INSERT or UPDATE of image/*, audio/*, video/* via ContentResolver with same URI re-written within short window; abnormal MIME/container change

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: HTTP(S)/QUIC media download with opaque content types (image/*, audio/*, video/*) from non-gallery domains or CDNs not previously used by the app

mutable_elements.description: Max time between media download/ingress, edit, and payload use/share (e.g., 10–120s depending on device performance).
Minimum Shannon entropy for edited media regions or container deltas (e.g., ≥ 7.1) to flag likely embedded payloads.
Minimum growth ratio between pre/post edit media (e.g., ≥ 1.25) to reduce noise from normal compression.
Minimum sequential small-write count to indicate chunked embedding or re-encode bursts.
List of atypical MIME/container transitions (e.g., PNG→JPEG with EXIF injection, WAV→M4A) for local tuning.
Trusted editors/camera apps allowed to perform frequent edits without alerting.
CDNs/domains expected to host user media for the enterprise; suppresses FP for legitimate apps.
Foreground, Work Profile, developer mode flags used to scope analytics.

strategies.name: Detection of Software Packing

analytics.name: Analytic 1721
analytics.description: From the defender view: a sandboxed process receives/creates a high-entropy Mach-O/bundle or encrypted segment, performs in-memory decrypt/unpack (mmap/mprotect RW→RX or RWX), optionally drops a transient image in app-writable dirs, then loads it through dyld/dlopen or spawns it. We correlate: (1) opaque blob write/arrival → (2) kernel memory protection changes → (3) dyld/dlopen from app-writable path or posix_spawn of a recently created image → (4) (optional) code-sign evaluation anomalies for the new image.

data_components.name: Module Load
data_components.channel: dlopen/image load from app-writable path (tmp, Caches) outside bundled resources

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: mmap/mprotect transitions to PROT_EXEC for pages associated with recently written files

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: Create/write of high-entropy Mach-O/bundle or generic blob in /var/mobile/Containers/Data/Application/<GUID>/(tmp|Library/Caches)/

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window from write→rwx→load/exec (e.g., 5–45s).
Entropy to flag packed blobs (e.g., ≥ 7.3).
Minimum RWX allocation size (e.g., ≥ 32KB).
Bundle IDs legitimately using JIT to avoid RWX false positives.
Regex for app-writable load paths (tmp, Caches) outside app bundle.
Tuning if enterprise/dev provisioning allows non-App Store binaries.

analytics.name: Analytic 1722
analytics.description: From the defender view: a sandboxed app handles a high-entropy executable blob, performs rapid decode/decrypt in memory (often with RW→RX or execmem friction), optionally emits a transient .dex/.so into app-writable paths, then immediately loads/executes it (DexClassLoader/dlopen) or spawns a helper. We correlate: (1) opaque blob write/arrival → (2) decode/unpack or memory protection change → (3) new code artifact or byte[] class definition → (4) dynamic load/exec within a tight window.

data_components.name: Module Load
data_components.channel: DexClassLoader/PathClassLoader loading from app-writable path OR reflective defineClass on byte[] payload

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: SELinux AVC for execmem/execute_no_trans/mprotect following recent writes by same UID

data_components.name: Process Creation
data_components.channel: dlopen of a recently created .so OR short-lived child (/system/bin/sh,toybox,linker) spawned by app_process

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: Create/write of high-entropy files in /data/data/<pkg>/(files|cache)/ or /storage/emulated/0/<...> with .dex/.so/.jar/.tmp/.bin

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window from write→unpack→load (e.g., 5–45s; device-dependent).
Entropy to flag packed blobs (e.g., ≥ 7.2).
Minimum RWX allocation size to reduce noise (e.g., ≥ 32KB).
Regex for suspicious .dex/.so/.jar/temp paths under app container.
Legit libraries/bundles expected to load from writable paths (test/dev builds).
Foreground/background, Work Profile, developer mode to scope alerts.

strategies.name: Detection of Download New Code at Runtime

analytics.name: Analytic 1677
analytics.description: From the defender’s view: an app retrieves opaque code (DEX/SO/JAR/JS) over the network or IPC, writes it into an app-writable path, optionally performs verification-bypass behaviors (reflection, addJavascriptInterface exposure, or execmem friction), and then loads/executes that code via DexClassLoader/PathClassLoader, dlopen, or WebView bridge invocation within a short window. The analytic correlates Network Content → File Creation/Modification → OS API Execution (loader/syscall/SELinux friction) → Module Load (DexClassLoader/dlopen) and, for WebView paths, Application Log signals of JavaScript interface attachment.

data_components.name: Module Load
data_components.channel: DexClassLoader|PathClassLoader load from app-writable path OR dlopen of a freshly created .so

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: SELinux AVC for execmem/execute_no_trans/mprotect following recent writes by same UID

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: Create/write under /data/data/<pkg>/(files|cache)/ or /storage/emulated/0/ with extension .dex/.jar/.so/.zip/.tmp/.js and elevated entropy

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: HTTP(S)/QUIC download of executable/opaque content (application/octet-stream, application/zip, application/java-archive, application/x-dex, application/x-sharedlib, text/javascript)

mutable_elements.description: Max correlation window between download → write → load (e.g., 10–60s depending on device/workload).
List of MIME types considered ‘code-like’ (octet-stream, zip, java-archive, x-dex, x-sharedlib, javascript).
Regex for app-writable destinations to watch (/data/data/<pkg>/(files|cache)/, /storage/emulated/0/...).
Entropy cutoff to flag likely code blobs (e.g., ≥ 7.2).
CDNs/domains expected for legitimate updates to reduce FPs.
Bundles/libs known to legitimately load from writable paths (dev/test apps).
Names of allowed WebView JS interfaces for the org (e.g., analytics only).
Foreground/background, Work Profile, dev mode to scope alerts.

analytics.name: Analytic 1678
analytics.description: From the defender’s view: a sandboxed app retrieves code-like content (JS/Mach-O/bundles), writes it to container tmp/Caches, performs memory permission changes (RW→RX/RWX) or directly loads via dyld/dlopen from writable paths, sometimes preceded by 3rd-party hotpatch frameworks (e.g., JSPatch-like behavior) or script engine evaluation. The analytic correlates Network Content → File Creation → OS API Execution (memory permission change) → Module Load (dyld/dlopen) and/or Process Access (codesign validation touches), with optional scripting engine events.

data_components.name: Module Load
data_components.channel: dlopen/image load from app-writable path (tmp, Caches) outside bundled resources

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: mmap/mprotect transitions to PROT_EXEC for pages associated with recently written files

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: Create/write in /var/mobile/Containers/Data/Application/<GUID>/(tmp|Library/Caches)/ for .js/.bundle/.dylib/.zip with elevated entropy

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: Per-App VPN flow with code-like content types (application/octet-stream, application/zip, text/javascript, application/x-mach-o)

mutable_elements.description: Max correlation window between download → write → load (e.g., 15–60s).
MIME list treated as code-like (octet-stream, zip, javascript, x-mach-o).
Regex for app container tmp/Caches writable paths.
Entropy cutoff to flag code blobs (e.g., ≥ 7.3).
Bundles that legitimately do JIT/script eval to reduce RWX noise.
Regex for loads from writable paths only (exclude app bundle).
Handle enterprise/dev-provisioned unsigned execution contexts.
Foreground/background or Work Profile state to filter noise.

strategies.name: Detection of Stored Application Data

analytics.name: Analytic 1683
analytics.description: Defender correlates an app escalating file visibility (permissions/flags, legacy storage modes) with enumeration of other apps’ storage or exported ContentProviders, followed by bulk reads/copies from target paths (including shared/external storage) and optional archive/encode then share/upload. Sequence: storage capability/permission gain → target discovery (provider queries, directory listing) → high-volume cross-app data reads from writable/shared paths → archive/encode → exfil/share within a short window.

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: QUERY on exported ContentProviders of other packages (content://<other.pkg>/*) or MediaStore scoped queries immediately preceding file reads

data_components.name: Process Access
data_components.channel: Runtime grant or manifest presence for MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE/READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE/READ_MEDIA_*; legacy external storage mode detection

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: CREATE/WRITE of archive or container (.zip/.gz/.7z/.db copy) that aggregates files pulled from other-package paths

data_components.name: File Access
data_components.channel: READ or COPY operations where path matches external/shared locations of other apps (e.g., /storage/emulated/0/Android/data/<otherpkg>/files/, /storage/emulated/0/Download/<app>/*)

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window to tie discovery → reads → package → exfil (e.g., 15–120s).
Regex for cross-app paths on external/shared storage to monitor.
List of exported/weakly-protected content providers under scrutiny.
Lower bound on cumulative read volume to avoid noisy single-file accesses.
Extensions considered packaging (.zip,.gz,.7z,.tar,.db copies).
Known good CDNs/APIs to reduce false positives.
Foreground/background, Work Profile, developer mode to scope alerts.

analytics.name: Analytic 1684
analytics.description: Defender correlates attempts to access other apps’ data via shared containers (App Groups), Photos/Files providers, pasteboard abuse, or jailbroken cross-container reads, followed by aggregation/packaging and optional exfil/share. Sequence: capability/consent (TCC/entitlements) → target discovery (AppGroup/Photos/Files enumeration, URL schemes) → bulk read from shared/foreign container or provider → package/encode → exfil/share.

data_components.name: Process Access
data_components.channel: Privacy (TCC) prompts/grants for Photos/Files or access changes indicating new visibility into user/app data

data_components.name: Application Log Content
data_components.channel: Repeated or large UIPasteboard reads; background pasteboard access shortly before packaging

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: CREATE/WRITE of archive/container (.zip/.gz/.7z/.db export) aggregating recently read items

data_components.name: File Access
data_components.channel: READ operations from App Group containers (/var/mobile/Containers/Shared/AppGroup/...) or Files/Photos provider mountpoints, especially when group not owned by bundle

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window for consent/discovery → read → package → exfil (e.g., 20–180s).
Allowed App Group IDs for each bundle to reduce FPs.
Files/Photos provider collections permitted for the app.
Lower bound on cumulative read size to signal collection vs casual access.
Packaging extensions to track when aggregating data.
Known-good enterprise domains/CDNs for uploads.
Foreground/background and Work Profile state to scope analytics.

strategies.name: Detection of Clipboard Data

analytics.name: Analytic 1719
analytics.description: From the defender view: an app registers a clipboard listener or calls ClipboardManager getters; the app is (a) foreground, (b) the default IME, or (c) abusing legacy paths. Shortly after each clipboard change, the app reads the primary clip repeatedly, optionally persists content (local file/DB) and/or exfiltrates it. We correlate: listener/clip-access → privilege/foreground confirmation → bursty reads → local write and/or network egress within a tight window.

data_components.name: Process Access
data_components.channel: Activity/Process state change (mFocusedApp, onResume/onPause) identifying <pkg> as foreground

data_components.name: Application Log Content
data_components.channel: Default IME active or bound to <pkg> (InputMethodManager reports imeId=<pkg>)

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: CREATE/WRITE to app-writable DB/file path indicating clipboard dump (e.g., clipboard.db, clip_*.txt)

mutable_elements.description: Max time between clip access → persist/exfil (e.g., 5–45s).
Minimum reads per clipboard change to flag harvesting (e.g., ≥2).
Regex for files/DBs used to stash clipboard content in app container.
Allowlisted domains to suppress false positives for analytics SDKs.
Require foreground unless app is the default IME (true/false).
Work Profile/Developer Mode/Doze to scope alerts.

analytics.name: Analytic 1720
analytics.description: From the defender view: an app accesses UIPasteboard contents, sometimes repeatedly, including in background or immediately after another app copies sensitive text. iOS 14+ shows user notifications when pasting cross-app; unified logs reflect pasteboard access, notification, and optional subsequent persistence/exfil. We correlate: pasteboard access → optional cross-app notification → local write (cache/DB) and/or network egress within a short window.

data_components.name: Process Access
data_components.channel: Foreground/background transition for <bundle_id> to contextualize access timing

data_components.name: Application Log Content
data_components.channel: UIPasteboard read (general/string/data) by <bundle_id>; repeated reads or background access

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: CREATE/WRITE of clipboard dump artifacts in container (clipboard.db, clip_*.txt, caches)

data_components.name: System Notifications
data_components.channel: \"has pasted from\" cross-app paste notification text containing source app name

mutable_elements.description: Max time between pasteboard access → persist/exfil (e.g., 5–60s).
Minimum reads within window to flag harvesting (e.g., ≥2).
Regex for paste dumps in app container.
Allowlisted analytics/CDN endpoints.
Require foreground state for benign use; flag background reads.
Work profile/MDM policy state to scope alerts.

strategies.name: Detection of Input Capture

analytics.name: Analytic 1825
analytics.description: Defender observes an app gaining input-observation capability (AccessibilityService enablement, default IME set, draw-over-apps permission), then creating an intercept surface (overlay window, accessibility event stream consumption or IME keystroke callbacks), followed by persistence (local keylog/clipboard dump) and/or small, frequent network egress. Chain: capability/permission → listener/overlay activation → bursty input read events → local write → near-term exfil.

data_components.name: Process Access
data_components.channel: Grant/activation of BIND_ACCESSIBILITY_SERVICE, BIND_INPUT_METHOD, SYSTEM_ALERT_WINDOW, POST_NOTIFICATIONS for <pkg>

data_components.name: Application Log Content
data_components.channel: Default IME changed/active: imeId=<pkg>, onStartInput/onFinishInput high frequency. TYPE_APPLICATION_OVERLAY|addView .* showing on top of package <otherPkg>

mutable_elements.description: Max time from input intercept to persist/exfil (e.g., 5–45s).
Minimum count of input events within window to flag harvesting (e.g., ≥5).
Require overlay creation if Accessibility not present (true/false).
Regex for keylog/clipboard dump destinations in app container.
Known-good analytics/CDN endpoints to suppress FPs.
Foreground/background/Work Profile or Kiosk policy to scope alerts.

analytics.name: Analytic 1826
analytics.description: Defender observes an app enabling or using input-capture surfaces (custom keyboard extension with Full Access, abnormal UI text entry interception, pasteboard polling adjacent to login screens), then persisting and/or exfiltrating captured input. Chain: capability/consent (TCC for keyboard Full Access or input privacy domains) → intercept behavior (keyboard extension active, repeated text field ‘editingChanged’/secure entry focus, background pasteboard reads) → local write → near-term egress.

data_components.name: Process Access
data_components.channel: Keyboard extension Full Access change; privacy grant touching input/keyboard categories for <bundle_id>

data_components.name: Application Log Content
data_components.channel: UIWindow/UIView events indicating secure text entry focus, editingChanged bursts, unexpected firstResponder cycling

data_components.name: File Creation
data_components.channel: CREATE/WRITE clipboard/keylog artifacts (clipboard.db, keys_*.txt) in container

mutable_elements.description: Max time from intercept to persist/exfil (e.g., 5–60s).
Minimum key/commit or editingChanged count to flag harvesting (e.g., ≥10).
Require keyboard Full Access to escalate severity (true/false).
Regex for keylog/clipboard dump files.
Known-good enterprise/analytics endpoints.
Foreground state, Focus modes, MDM policy.

strategies.name: Detection of Keylogging

analytics.name: Analytic 1751
analytics.description: Defender correlates an app acquiring input-capture capability (AccessibilityService enablement or default IME set) with high-frequency text-change/IME commit callbacks sourced from other packages, followed by local keylog persistence and/or small, immediate network egress. Chain: capability/permission → intercept (accessibility ‘TYPE_VIEW_TEXT_CHANGED’ or IME commitText/onStartInput bursts) → persist to container → near-term egress.

data_components.channel: Default IME active imeId=<pkg>; frequent onStartInput/commitText calls

Minimum input events in window to flag (e.g., ≥10).

Enterprise/analytics endpoints to suppress FPs.

analytics.name: Analytic 1752
analytics.description: Defender correlates a custom keyboard extension activation (optionally with TCC ‘Full Access’) or abnormal UI text-entry interception with local keylog persistence and/or small egress. Chain: capability/consent (keyboard Full Access/TCC) → intercept (keyboard commit events or repeated secure text entry edits) → persist to container → near-term egress.

strategies.name: Detection of GUI Input Capture

analytics.name: Analytic 1778
analytics.description: Defender correlates an app preparing to phish (gaining overlay/notification/accessibility capability) with precise foreground targeting (reading activity in front via accessibility/focus) and then presenting a look-alike UI (overlay window or activity-on-top) immediately before local storage or small-burst egress of entered data. Chain: capability/permission → target app in foreground detected → overlay/activity-on-top or fake notification tap → local prompt input write → near-term network egress.

data_components.channel: TYPE_WINDOW_STATE_CHANGED / TYPE_VIEW_FOCUSED shows foreign target package in foreground

Known-good analytics/CDN/service domains to suppress FPs.

strategies.name: Detection of Process Discovery

analytics.name: Analytic 1804
analytics.description: Defender observes an app/package attempting to enumerate running processes by triggering restricted process visibility mechanisms (e.g., repeated queries for running tasks/services, rapid iteration over process identifiers, or access attempts against /proc entries) that are atypical for its declared function and occur without an associated user-facing diagnostic workflow. The detection relies on correlating (1) OS/API calls or shell/system utility execution indicative of process listing or /proc traversal, (2) app privilege context (root, debug build, device owner/profile owner, accessibility/IME status), (3) background execution state, and (4) optional follow-on behaviors consistent with automated discovery (short bursts of local IPC probes, network beacons immediately after enumeration, or rapid targeting of specific high-value package/process names). The analytic should describe what is observable: repeated enumeration signals + privilege context + timing relationship, not the adversary’s intent.

strategies.name: Detection of SIM Card Swap

analytics.name: Analytic 1747
analytics.description: A defender correlates a sudden carrier identity/service state change (SIM/line identifier change or unexpected loss of cellular service) with near-term device messaging/telephony disruption and a concurrent shift in authentication traffic patterns—such as a spike in SMS-based verification flows or account recovery activity from the same user’s identities—indicating the user’s number may have been transferred to a different SIM/device (SIM swap impact).

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: Agent-observable telephony subscription/state API signals indicating SIM/eSIM subscription change (vendor-agnostic: 'telephony subscription changed')

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: Abrupt shift from cellular egress to Wi-Fi-only egress, or new VPN/proxy session establishment following cellular service loss

data_components.name: Network Traffic Content
data_components.channel: Near-term increase in traffic to identity endpoints associated with SMS MFA, account recovery, or OTP verification (IdP, banking, crypto), correlated to SIM/service loss

data_components.name: Application Permission
data_components.channel: Device inventory changes involving phone number/line identifier fields (when available), eSIM profile presence, or compliance signal indicating SIM profile change

data_components.name: System Settings
data_components.channel: Cellular service state transitions (in-service→no-service), SIM state change, carrier/operator identifier change, or baseband/telephony stack state change observed by agent telemetry

mutable_elements.description: Minimum duration of unexpected cellular service loss before considering it suspicious (reduces noise from transient coverage issues).
Which SIM-related state changes to alert on (SIM removed, SIM refresh, operator changed, eSIM profile changed).
Time window to correlate SIM/service state change with downstream identity traffic anomalies (e.g., 30m–6h).
Baseline of expected IdP/banking/crypto identity endpoints for the org; used to reduce false positives.
Threshold for increase in OTP/MFA/account recovery traffic volume relative to user baseline.
Optional enrichment—treat carrier changes as lower risk during known travel/roaming windows.

analytics.name: Analytic 1748
analytics.description: A defender correlates an unexpected change in cellular subscription state (eSIM/SIM profile change, carrier/operator change, or sudden persistent loss of cellular service) with near-term disruption signals and a rapid increase in authentication-related network activity consistent with SMS verification or account recovery flows, suggesting the user’s number has been ported to an adversary-controlled SIM/device (SIM swap impact).

strategies.name: Detection of Abuse Accessibility Features

analytics.name: Analytic 1812
analytics.description: A defender correlates an application being granted accessibility service control with subsequent consumption of high-volume accessibility events, interaction with sensitive UI elements or text-entry fields, optional overlay/window presentation over other applications, and near-term local buffering or outbound network transmission, indicating abuse of accessibility features for input capture, credential theft, or automated interaction.

strategies.name: Detection of Drive-By Compromise

analytics.name: Analytic 1669
analytics.description: A defender correlates navigation to external web content in a browser or embedded WebView with immediate script-heavy or exploit-preparation network activity, followed by abnormal browser/WebView process behavior, suspicious file or download artifacts, or rapid post-visit capability shifts such as new package install attempts, overlay prompts, permission requests, or outbound command traffic inconsistent with normal browsing.

analytics.name: Analytic 1802

analytics.description: Defender correlates a chain where a device establishes a new trusted USB host pairing or enters developer/debug configuration state, followed by device data extraction activity, configuration manipulation, or abnormal application behavior shortly after the pairing event.

strategies.name: Detection of Lockscreen Bypass

analytics.description: A lock-state transition telemetry, special access or privileged interaction capability, security-sensitive framework use, and immediate downstream activity while the user-interaction context is weak or inconsistent. This yields stronger coverage on Android than iOS.

Apps expected to access camera or other sensors near the authentication boundary.

analytics.name: Analytic 1724
analytics.description: Defender correlates an iOS-specific reduced-confidence chain where a supervised or managed device transitions from locked or inactive state to interactive or application-active state with weak evidence of expected user authentication, often accompanied by abnormal protected posture change, trust-state change, unexpected app wake, sensor use, or immediate downstream communication. Because direct visibility into lockscreen bypass mechanics on iOS is limited, the analytic prioritizes strong device-state effects and post-unlock behavior rather than pretending to observe the exact bypass method.

strategies.name: Detection of Network Denial of Service

analytics.name: Analytic 1713
analytics.description: Defender correlates an Android-specific causal chain where device connectivity degrades or oscillates across one or more radios, applications lose or repeatedly reattempt network access, and the radio or network failure pattern is inconsistent with ordinary mobility, coverage transition, or user-initiated airplane mode behavior. The defender correlates radio state, connectivity framework behavior, application state, network session failures, and location/network-provider degradation to distinguish network denial effects from routine weak-signal conditions.

data_components.channel: Connectivity manager, telephony, Wi-Fi, network callback, or location-provider framework reports repeated unavailable, disconnected, suspended, or degraded state transitions

Time threshold for determining whether connectivity degradation occurred during active device use versus idle background operation.
Threshold for repeated disconnects, resets, DNS failures, or transport failures within the correlation window.
Apps or services expected to rely on GPS or network-based location and therefore likely to exhibit secondary degradation during jamming.
Known sites or geographies with weak legitimate coverage that should be baseline-adjusted.

analytics.name: Analytic 1714
analytics.description: Defender correlates an iOS-specific reduced-confidence chain where a managed or supervised device remains active but experiences abrupt loss of network-dependent functionality, repeated session failure, or sustained communication inability without matching configuration changes or ordinary user action. Because direct radio-layer and RF-cause visibility is weaker on iOS, the defender emphasizes device posture, application wake or foreground behavior during service loss, protected network-policy stability, and downstream failure patterns observed in VPN or proxy telemetry.

data_components.channel: Observed network-path, reachability, DNS, transport, or location-provider framework reports repeated unavailable or failed state near active device use

data_components.name: Protected Configuration
data_components.channel: Managed Wi-Fi, VPN, cellular, or location-service policy remains unchanged while device connectivity repeatedly degrades

Threshold for repeated session failures, resets, timeouts, or DNS failures within the correlation window.
Known sites or geographies where benign poor service should be baseline-adjusted.
Expected enterprise destinations whose temporary maintenance or outage should not be treated as device-targeted denial.

strategies.name: Detection of Data Encrypted for Impact

analytics.name: Analytic 1781
analytics.description: An application with access to broad file scopes or sensitive storage areas becomes active, performs abnormal burst file reads and writes across many user or shared-storage locations, transforms file content or extensions at scale in a short window, and causes rapid file inaccessibility, rewrite, or replacement inconsistent with normal sync, backup, media processing, or document-editing behavior. The defender correlates capability state, app lifecycle, framework use, bulk file-write effects, and optional network communications to distinguish encrypt-for-impact behavior from benign bulk file operations.

data_components.channel: Content resolver, document provider, media store, storage access framework, bulk stream processing, or repeated crypto-adjacent framework use observed during multi-file transformation

data_components.name: Application Permission

data_components.name: Protected Configuration

Threshold for number of file create, overwrite, rename, or replace actions within the correlation window.

Threshold for cumulative bytes written during the impact window.
Known paths, document roots, or work-profile storage locations where benign enterprise migration or sync tooling may rewrite many files.
Expected network destinations contacted by legitimate storage, sync, backup, or MDM remediation apps.

strategies.name: Detection of Supply Chain Compromise

analytics.name: Analytic 1697
analytics.description: An app or app update arrives through an expected delivery path or presents as a known legitimate package identity, but its post-install or post-update behavior materially changes in ways inconsistent with its historical role. The defender correlates package identity and install/update context, newly expanded capability state, changed runtime framework use, new sensor or storage behaviors, and new network destinations shortly after installation or update to identify likely supply-chain compromise rather than ordinary malicious sideloading or unrelated post-compromise activity.

mutable_elements.description: Maximum span between app install/update event and first suspicious post-delivery behavior.

Whether certain behaviors should only be considered suspicious when they occur without visible user interaction.

Expected new destinations, APIs, CDNs, or telemetry endpoints associated with approved app updates.
Threshold for how many newly added or newly exercised permissions/capabilities are considered abnormal for a known app.
Population of prior devices, versions, or user cohorts used to baseline normal app behavior.

analytics.description: A managed or supervised app, app update, or enterprise-distributed build retains a legitimate-seeming identity but exhibits post-delivery behavior inconsistent with its expected role, prior version, or distribution context. Because iOS exposes less direct visibility into bundled dependency tampering or component-level supply-chain insertion, the defender prioritizes supervised app inventory, signing/provisioning trust posture, entitlement and behavior drift after update, new sensor/resource use, and new downstream network effects soon after install or version change.

analytics.description: The defender observes a newly enrolled or recently activated device presenting abnormal integrity, hardware-backed attestation, or firmware/build relationships at the management plane, followed by privileged or system-context access to protected resources or framework paths, and then outbound communication inconsistent with setup state, lock state, or recent user interaction. The causal sequence is strongest when the device has not yet reached a normal trusted posture but still exhibits system-level capability use or network activity.

strategies.name: Detection of User Evasion

analytics.description: Correlates (1) continuous or repeated use of motion or interaction-inference signals that do not require overt user-facing privilege prompts, (2) suppression of higher-risk behavior while user presence or active handling is inferred, and (3) resumption of background execution, sensor use, local data handling, or network activity only when device interaction falls below a threshold. The defender observes a causal chain where an application senses user/device interaction state and intentionally gates malicious behavior to user-inactive periods.

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: application invokes motion-sensor or device-activity framework operations followed by conditional execution of sensitive framework activity only after inferred user absence

data_components.name: Application State
data_components.channel: application reduces or halts operational activity during periods of active user interaction and resumes background execution or periodic work only during low-motion or idle intervals

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window between motion-state inference and subsequent deferred execution
Threshold defining when device motion or interaction is considered low enough to permit hidden execution
Environment-specific set of motion or activity signals used to infer user presence
Baseline of legitimate applications expected to use motion or activity sensing while also conditionally changing behavior
Whether suspiciousness increases when deferred activity starts from background or with no recent foreground interaction
Minimum outbound traffic threshold used to distinguish meaningful deferred operation from benign maintenance traffic

strategies.name: Detection of Impair Defenses

analytics.name: Analytic 1797
analytics.description: Correlates (1) application-driven modification of device security posture or monitoring capability (e.g., accessibility abuse, disabling security app components, altering monitoring configuration), (2) immediate degradation or cessation of expected telemetry sources such as mobile EDR, sensor visibility, or system monitoring, and (3) subsequent application activity continuing with reduced observability. The defender observes a causal chain where defensive visibility or enforcement is altered first, followed by continued execution under reduced monitoring conditions.

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: application invokes system framework operations that alter monitoring, accessibility, or execution visibility followed by reduction in expected telemetry generation

data_components.name: Application Permission
data_components.channel: change to security-relevant device configuration or managed policy (e.g., accessibility enablement, app admin changes, security service state change) preceding telemetry degradation

data_components.name: Application State
data_components.channel: ecurity or monitoring application transitions to disabled, inactive, or non-reporting state while other applications remain active

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window between configuration change, telemetry degradation, and subsequent activity
Baseline set of telemetry sources expected to report continuously (EDR, sensor feeds, monitoring services)
Duration or volume threshold defining abnormal loss of telemetry
Applications legitimately capable of modifying device configuration or security posture
Set of security-relevant controls considered high-impact if altered (EDR, accessibility, admin APIs)
Outbound traffic threshold used to confirm continued activity during telemetry loss

strategies.name: Detection of Prevent Application Removal

analytics.name: Analytic 1644
analytics.description: Correlates (1) an application obtaining or maintaining elevated control mechanisms capable of resisting removal (device administrator, accessibility control, managed-owner posture), (2) user navigation into uninstall or application-management flows, and (3) immediate UI redirection, back-navigation injection, modal dismissal, or failed uninstall completion followed by continued app presence. Defender observes a causal chain where a removal attempt is actively disrupted and the target application remains installed.

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: application invokes accessibility global actions (back/home/recents) or observes package-management UI immediately after uninstall/settings screen becomes foreground

data_components.name: Application Permission
data_components.channel: application enabled as device administrator, device owner, profile owner, or equivalent elevated management role before uninstall attempt

data_components.name: Application Permission
data_components.channel: application granted accessibility service privileges capable of screen observation or global action invocation before removal attempt

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window between uninstall UI entry, interference event, and continued install state
Set of elevated roles considered removal-resistant (device admin, owner modes, accessibility)
UI actions considered suspicious during uninstall flows (BACK, HOME, RECENTS)
Known legitimate accessibility services expected to use global actions
Number of repeated uninstall attempts before escalation
Outbound traffic threshold confirming continued meaningful activity after failed removal

strategies.name: Detection of Device Lockout

analytics.name: Analytic 1652
analytics.description: Correlates (1) acquisition or presence of elevated control paths capable of forcing a lock state or blocking user interaction, (2) invocation of screen-locking or UI-denial behavior such as DevicePolicyManager lock operations, persistent overlays, accessibility-driven navigation interruption, or foreground lock-screen impersonation, and (3) immediate transition of the device into an unavailable or repeatedly re-locked state while the responsible application remains installed and active. The defender observes a causal chain where an application first gains the ability to control lock-related behavior, then forces or simulates lockout, and the device becomes unusable to the legitimate user.

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: application invokes lock-related or UI-denial framework operations, including DevicePolicyManager lock actions, persistent overlay behavior, or accessibility-driven navigation interference immediately before device enters locked or unusable state

data_components.name: Application Permission
data_components.channel: application enabled as device administrator, device owner, or profile owner before screen-lock or password-control activity

data_components.name: Application Permission
data_components.channel: application granted accessibility service privileges capable of intercepting UI flow or sustaining user-interaction denial before lockout event

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window between privileged control acquisition, lockout action, and resulting device lock state
Set of elevated roles that materially increase lockout capability, such as device admin, device owner, profile owner, or accessibility service
Framework actions treated as lockout-relevant, including lockNow, password-control changes, overlay persistence, and UI-denial actions
Baseline of legitimate enterprise or security apps expected to invoke lock-related controls
Number of repeated lock or lock-like transitions in a short interval required before escalation
Outbound traffic threshold confirming continued meaningful activity after lockout

strategies.name: Detection of Disable or Modify Tools

analytics.name: Analytic 1806
analytics.description: Correlates (1) application acquisition or use of elevated control paths capable of altering defensive tooling or protected system state, such as device administration, root-enabled modification, or security-setting manipulation, (2) direct changes to security-tool configuration, service state, package state, or protected enforcement settings such as SELinux-relevant files or security-app components, and (3) immediate degradation, suppression, or disappearance of expected security telemetry while the device and initiating application remain active. The defender observes a causal chain where a security control is modified first, then monitoring or protection weakens, and subsequent activity continues under reduced defensive visibility.

data_components.channel: application invokes package, settings, or privileged framework operations capable of disabling security software, altering security enforcement, or interfering with reporting before telemetry loss

data_components.name: File Creation

data_components.name: Application Permission

data_components.name: Application Permission
data_components.channel: security-relevant application package state, enabled status, administrator state, or managed protection setting changes immediately before monitoring degradation

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window between security-setting change, tool degradation, and subsequent continued activity

Duration or volume threshold defining abnormal loss of expected security telemetry
Protected settings or files treated as suspicious if modified, including SELinux-relevant enforcement state or security-app configuration
Legitimate applications or management agents allowed to modify security-relevant posture
Outbound traffic threshold used to confirm continued meaningful activity during reduced defensive visibility

strategies.name: Detection of Indicator Removal on Host

analytics.name: Analytic 1733
analytics.description: Detects indirect evidence of host-side indicator removal by correlating (1) local artifact creation or compromise-state-relevant activity, (2) later disappearance, alteration, or reporting loss for those artifacts or state indicators, and (3) continued application or device activity under reduced visibility. Because iOS provides weaker direct visibility into some Android-style artifact and jailbreak-indicator manipulation patterns, the defender relies more on app-private artifact lifecycle changes, managed posture shifts, and continued runtime or network activity after expected evidence disappears.

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window between artifact disappearance, posture change, and continued activity

Threshold defining abnormal loss of artifact visibility or managed-state continuity

Outbound traffic threshold used to confirm meaningful continued activity after indicator removal

analytics.name: Analytic 1734
analytics.description: Correlates (1) application activity that creates, modifies, or accesses local artifacts relevant to detection or device compromise state, (2) subsequent deletion, alteration, renaming, relocation, or visibility suppression of those artifacts, including files, application presence, media, or root-compromise indicators, and (3) continued application execution, reduced telemetry quality, or outbound activity after the artifact state changes. The defender observes a causal chain where host-side evidence is first manipulated and expected visibility or reporting degrades while the initiating application remains active.

Legitimate apps expected to delete or alter artifacts as part of normal lifecycle or cleanup behavior
Outbound traffic threshold used to confirm meaningful activity after indicator removal

strategies.name: Detection of Uninstall Malicious Application

analytics.name: Analytic 1801
analytics.description: Correlates (1) a malicious application gaining or using a removal-capable control path, such as device owner or delegated app-management authority, accessibility service control over uninstall UI, or rooted filesystem access, (2) initiation of uninstall or package-removal behavior, and (3) disappearance of the application from installed-state inventory or app runtime immediately afterward, often with a short-lived final burst of local cleanup or outbound communication. The defender observes a causal chain where the application first establishes the ability to remove itself, then triggers uninstall or deletion, and then vanishes from expected app presence while device activity continues.

data_components.name: OS API Execution
data_components.channel: application invokes uninstall-related package-management operations, accessibility-driven uninstall confirmation actions, or privileged file-removal operations immediately before installed-state loss

data_components.name: File Deletion
data_components.channel: application deletes package files, cleanup artifacts, or app-local state immediately before disappearance from installed inventory or runtime

data_components.name: Application Permission
data_components.channel: application has accessibility service privileges immediately before package-removal UI flow and subsequent application disappearance

data_components.name: Application Permission
data_components.channel: application holds device-owner, profile-owner, or delegated app-management authority capable of package removal before uninstall event

data_components.name: Application Permission
data_components.channel: device posture indicates rooted, compromised, or non-compliant state before package files disappear without standard managed uninstall workflow

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window between uninstall-capable control, removal action, and app disappearance
Roles or privileges considered capable of enabling silent or assisted uninstall, such as device owner, delegated app-management authority, accessibility, or rooted filesystem access
Legitimate enterprise or device-management apps allowed to uninstall applications
Signals used to recognize uninstall initiation, such as package-removal actions, uninstall intent flows, or accessibility-driven confirmation steps
Maximum time between removal action and loss of installed-state visibility
Outbound traffic threshold used to confirm final activity before self-removal

strategies.name: Detection of File Deletion

analytics.name: Analytic 1712
analytics.description: Correlates (1) application access to or staging of local files likely to be of operational, evidentiary, or user value, (2) deletion of those files or wipe-like destructive actions through ordinary storage access, administrative controls, or privileged/rooted paths, and (3) continued app or device activity after deletion, including cleanup, concealment, or outbound transfer. The defender observes a causal chain where files are first accessed or prepared, then removed, and device-side behavior continues after evidence or data is gone.

mutable_elements.description: Correlation window between file access or staging, deletion event, and subsequent activity

strategies.name: Detection of Subvert Trust Controls

analytics.name: Analytic 1745
analytics.description:
On Android, the user can use the device settings menu to view trusted CA certificates and look for unexpected or unknown certificates. A mobile security product could similarly examine the trusted CA certificate store for anomalies. Users can use the device settings menu to view which applications on the device are allowed to install unknown applications.

On iOS, the user can use the device settings menu to view installed Configuration Profiles and look for unexpected or unknown profiles. A Mobile Device Management (MDM) system could use the iOS MDM APIs to examine the list of installed Configuration Profiles for anomalies.

analytics.name: Analytic 1744
analytics.description:
When vetting applications for potential security weaknesses, the vetting process could look for insecure use of Intents. Developers should be encouraged to use techniques to ensure that the intent can only be sent to an appropriate destination (e.g., use explicit rather than implicit intents, permission checking, checking of the destination app's signing certificate, or utilizing the App Links feature). For mobile applications using OAuth, encourage use of best practice.(Citation: IETF-OAuthNativeApps)(Citation: Android-AppLinks)
On Android, users may be presented with a popup to select the appropriate application to open a URI in. If the user sees an application they do not recognize, they can remove it.

strategies.name: Detection of Adversary-in-the-Middle

analytics.name: Analytic 1687
analytics.description:
Mobile security products can potentially detect rogue Wi-Fi access points if the adversary is attempting to decrypt traffic using an untrusted SSL certificate. 
Application vetting services should look for applications that request VPN access. These applications should be heavily scrutinized since VPN functionality is not very common. 
On both Android and iOS, the user must grant consent to an application to act as a VPN. Both platforms also provide visual context to the user in the top status bar when a VPN connection is active. The user can see registered VPN services in the device settings.

strategies.name: Detection of Data from Information Repositories

analytics.name: Analytic 1886
analytics.description:
Monitor for newly constructed logon behavior within Microsoft's SharePoint can be configured to report access to certain pages and documents.(Citation: Microsoft SharePoint Logging) Sharepoint audit logging can also be configured to report when a user shares a resource.(Citation: Sharepoint Sharing Events) The user access logging within Atlassian's Confluence can also be configured to report access to certain pages and documents through AccessLogFilter.(Citation: Atlassian Confluence Logging) Additional log storage and analysis infrastructure will likely be required for more robust detection capabilities. 
In the case of detecting collection from shared network drives monitor for unexpected and abnormal accesses to network shares. 
Monitor for third-party application logging, messaging, and/or other artifacts that may leverage information repositories to mine valuable information. Information repositories generally have a considerably large user base, detection of malicious use can be non-trivial. At minimum, access to information repositories performed by privileged users (for example, Active Directory Domain, Enterprise, or Schema Administrators) should be closely monitored and alerted upon, as these types of accounts should generally not be used to access information repositories. If the capability exists, it may be of value to monitor and alert on users that are retrieving and viewing a large number of documents and pages; this behavior may be indicative of programmatic means being used to retrieve all data within the repository. In environments with high-maturity, it may be possible to leverage User-Behavioral Analytics (UBA) platforms to detect and alert on user-based anomalies.

For added context on adversary enterprise procedures and background see [Remote System Discovery](https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1018).

strategies.name: Detection of Multicast Discovery

analytics.name: Analytic 2052
analytics.description:
Monitor for anomalies related to discovery related ICS functions, including devices that have not previously used these functions or for functions being sent to many outstations.
